entries.4f3fc63d711010282bc3a5de264fd1770c1a210a: <div sID="gen15528" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Isa.5" sID="Isa.5"/> <div eID="gen15528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15529" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15530" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophet, in God's name, shows the people of God their transgressions, even the house of Jacob their sins, and the judgments which were likely to be brought upon them for their sins, I. By a parable, under the similitude of an unfruitful vineyard, representing the great favours God had bestowed upon them, their disappointing his expectations from them, and the ruin they had thereby deserved, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. By an enumeration of the sins that did abound among them, with a threatening of punishments that should answer to the sins. 1. Covetousness, and greediness of worldly wealth, which shall be punished with famine, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8-Isa.5.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 2. Rioting, revelling, and drunkenness (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11-Isa.5.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">23</reference>), which shall be punished with captivity and all the miseries that attend it, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13-Isa.5.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. 3. Presumption in sin, and defying the justice of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.18-Isa.5.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>. 4. Confounding the distinctions between virtue and vice, and so undermining the principles of religion, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">ver. 20</reference>. 5. Self-conceit, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.21">ver. 21</reference>. 6. Perverting justice, for which, and the other instances of reigning wickedness among them, a great and general desolation in threatened, which should lay all waste (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.24-Isa.5.25">ver. 24, 25</reference>), and which should be effected by a foreign invasion (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26-Isa.5.30">ver. 26-30</reference>), referring perhaps to the havoc made not long after by Sennacherib's army.
entries.227eada46680823ec7b8d6394caa424af546d1db: <div eID="gen15530" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15529" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel Compared to a Vineyard. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15531" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: <hi type="super">2</hi> And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes. <hi type="super">3</hi> And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. <hi type="super">4</hi> What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? <hi type="super">5</hi> And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; <hi type="italic">and</hi> break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. <hi type="super">7</hi> For the vineyard of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. <div eID="gen15531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15532" type="x-p"/> See what variety of methods the great God takes to awaken sinners to repentance by convincing them of sin, and showing them their misery and danger by reason of it. To this purport he speaks sometimes in plain terms and sometimes in parables, sometimes in prose and sometimes in verse, as here. "We have tried to <hi type="italic">reason with you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>); now let us put your case into a poem, inscribed to the honour of my well beloved." God the Father dictates it to the honour of Christ his well beloved Son, whom he has constituted Lord of the vineyard. The prophet sings it to the honour of Christ too, for he is his well beloved. The Old-Testament prophets were friends of the bridegroom. Christ is God's beloved Son and our beloved Saviour. Whatever is said or sung of the church must be intended to his praise, even that which (like this) tends to our shame. This parable was put into a song that it might be the more moving and affecting, might be the more easily learned and exactly remembered, and the better transmitted to posterity; and it is an exposition of he song of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.1-Deut.32.47">Deut. xxxii.</reference>), showing that what he then foretold was now fulfilled. Jerome says, Christ the well-beloved did in effect sing this mournful song when he beheld Jerusalem <hi type="italic">and wept over it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.41">Luke xix. 41</reference>), and had reference to it in the parable of the vineyard (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.33">Matt. xxi. 33</reference>, &c.), only here the fault was in the vines, there in the husbandmen. Here we have, <div eID="gen15532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15533" type="x-p"/> I. The great things which God had done for the Jewish church and nation. When all the rest of the world lay in common, not cultivated by divine revelation, that was his vineyard, they were his peculiar people. He acknowledged them as his own, set them apart for himself. The soil they were planted in was extraordinary; it was <hi type="italic">a very fruitful hill, the horn of the son of oil;</hi> so it is in the margin. There was plenty, a cornucopia; and there was dainty: they did there eat the fat and drink the sweet, and so were furnished with abundance of good things to honour God with in sacrifices and free-will offerings. The advantages of our situation will be brought into the account another day. Observe further what God did for this vineyard. 1. He fenced it, took it under his special protection, kept it night and day under his own eye, lest any should hurt it, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.3">ch. xxvii. 2, 3</reference>. If they had not themselves thrown down their fence, no inroad could have been made upon them, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Ps. cxxv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.131.4">cxxxi. 4</reference>. 2. He gathered the stones out of it, that, as nothing from without might damage it, so nothing within might obstruct its fruitfulness. He proffered his grace to take away the stony heart. 3. He planted it with the choicest vine, set up a pure religion among them, gave them a most excellent law, instituted ordinances very proper for the keeping up of their acquaintance with God, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer. ii. 21</reference>. 4. He built a tower in the midst of it, either for defence against violence or for the dressers of the vineyard to lodge in; or rather it was for the owner of the vineyard to sit in, to take a view of the vines (<reference osisRef="Song.7.12">Cant. vii. 12</reference>)—a summer-house. The temple was this tower, about which the priests lodged, and where God promised to meet his people, and gave them the tokens of his presence among them and pleasure in them. 5. He made a wine-press therein, set up his altar, to which the sacrifices, as the fruits of the vineyard, should be brought. <div eID="gen15533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15534" type="x-p"/> II. The disappointment of his just expectations from them: <hi type="italic">He looked that it should bring forth grapes,</hi> and a great deal of reason he had for that expectation. Note, God expects vineyard-fruit from those that enjoy vineyard-privileges, not leaves only, as <reference osisRef="Mark.11.12">Mark xi. 12</reference>. A bare profession, though ever so green, will not serve: there must be more than buds and blossoms. Good purposes and good beginnings are good things, but not enough; there must be fruit, a good heart and a good life, vineyard fruit, thoughts and affections, words and actions, agreeable to the Spirit, which is the fatness of the vineyard (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22-Gal.5.23">Gal. v. 22, 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">answerable to the ordinances,</hi> which are the dressings of the vineyard, acceptable to God, the Lord of the vineyard, and fruit according to the season. Such fruit as this God expects from us, grapes, the fruit of the vine, with which they honour God and man (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.13">Judg. ix. 13</reference>); and his expectations are neither high nor hard, but righteous and very reasonable. Yet see how his expectations are frustrated: <hi type="italic">It brought forth wild grapes;</hi> not only no fruit at all, but bad fruit, worse than none, grapes of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deut. xxxii. 32</reference>. 1. Wild grapes are the fruits of the corrupt nature, fruit according to the crabstock, not according to the engrafted branch, from the root of bitterness, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">Heb. xii. 15</reference>. Where grace does not work corruption will. 2. Wild grapes are hypocritical performances in religion, that look like grapes, but are sour or bitter, and are so far from being pleasing to God that they are provoking, as theirs mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>. Counterfeit graces are wild grapes. <div eID="gen15534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15535" type="x-p"/> III. An appeal to themselves whether upon the whole matter God must not be justified and they condemned, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3-Isa.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. And now the case is plainly stated: <hi type="italic">O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah! judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard.</hi> This implies that God was blamed about them. There was a controversy between them and him; but the equity was so plain on his side that he could venture to put the decision of the controversy to their own consciences. "Let any inhabitant of Jerusalem, any man of Judah, that has but the use of his reason and a common sense of equity and justice, speak his mind impartially in this matter." Here is a challenge to any man to show, 1. Any instance wherein God had been wanting to them: <hi type="italic">What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?</hi> He speaks of the external means of fruitfulness, and such as might be expected from the dresser of a vineyard, from whom it is not required that he should change the nature of the vine. <hi type="italic">What ought to have been done more?</hi> so it may be read. They had everything requisite for instruction and direction in their duty, for quickening them to it and putting them in mind of it. No inducements were wanting to persuade them to it, but all arguments were used that were proper to work either upon hope or fear; and they had all the opportunities they could desire for the performance of their duty, the new moons, and the sabbaths, and solemn feasts; They had the scriptures, the lively oracles, a standing ministry in the priests and Levites, besides what was extraordinary in the prophets. No nation had statutes and judgments so righteous. 2. Nor could any tolerable excuse be offered for their walking thus contrary to God. "Wherefore, what reason can be given why it should bring forth wild grapes, when I looked for grapes?" Note, The wickedness of those that profess religion, and enjoy the means of grace, is the most unreasonable unaccountable thing in the world, and the whole blame of it must lie upon the sinners themselves. "<hi type="italic">If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it,</hi> and shalt not have a word to say for thyself in the judgment of the great day." God will prove his own ways equal and the sinner's ways unequal. <div eID="gen15535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15536" type="x-p"/> IV. Their doom read, and a righteous sentence passed upon them for their bad conduct towards God (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.5-Isa.5.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">And now go to,</hi> since nothing can be offered in excuse of the crime or arrest of the judgement, <hi type="italic">I will tell you what I am now determined to do to my vineyard.</hi> I will be vexed and troubled with it no more; since it will be good for nothing, it <hi type="italic">shall</hi> be good for nothing; in short, it shall cease to be a vineyard, and be turned into a wilderness: the church of the Jews shall be unchurched; their charter shall be taken away, and they shall become <hi type="italic">lo-ammi—not my people.</hi>" 1. "They shall no longer be distinguished as a peculiar people, but be laid in common: <hi type="italic">I will take away the hedge thereof,</hi> and then it will soon be eaten up and become as bare as other ground." They mingled with the nations and therefore were justly scattered among them. 2. "They shall no longer be protected as God's people, but left exposed. God will not only suffer the wall to go to decay, but he will break it down, will remove all their defences from them, and then they will become an easy prey to their enemies, who have long waited for an opportunity to do them a mischief, and will now tread them down and trample upon them." 3. "They shall no longer have the face of a vineyard, and the form and shape of a church and commonwealth, but shall be levelled and laid waste." This was fulfilled when <hi type="italic">Jerusalem for their sakes was ploughed as a field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>. 4. "No more pains shall be taken with them by magistrates or ministers, the dressers and keepers of their vineyard; it shall not be pruned nor digged, but every thing shall run wild, and nothing shall come up but briers and thorns, the products of sin and the curse," <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>. When errors and corruptions, vice and immorality, go without check or control, no testimony borne against them, no rebuke given them or restraint put upon them, the vineyard is unpruned, is not dressed, or ridded; and then it will soon be like the vineyard of the man void of understanding, all grown over with thorns. 5. "That which completes its woe is that the dews of heaven shall be withheld; he that has the key of the clouds will command them that they rain no rain upon it, and that alone is sufficient to run it into a desert." Note, God in a way of righteous judgment, denies his grace to those that have long received it in vain. The sum of all is that those who would not bring forth good fruit should bring forth none. The curse of barrenness is the punishment of the sin of barrenness, as <reference osisRef="Mark.11.14">Mark xi. 14</reference>. This had its partial accomplishment in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, its full accomplishment in the final rejection of the Jews, and has its frequent accomplishment in the departure of God's Spirit from those persons who have long resisted him and striven against him, and the removal of his gospel from those places that have been long a reproach to it, while it has been an honour to them. It is no loss to God to lay his vineyard waste; for he can, when he please, turn a wilderness into a fruitful field; and when he does thus dismantle a vineyard, it is but as he did by the garden of Eden, which, when man had by sin forfeited his place in it, was soon levelled with common soil. <div eID="gen15536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15537" type="x-p"/> V. The explanation of this parable, or a key to it (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">v. 7</reference>), where we are told, 1. What is meant by the vineyard (it is <hi type="italic">the house of Israel,</hi> the body of the people, incorporated in one church and commonwealth), and what by the vines, the pleasant plants, the plants of God's pleasure, which he had been pleased in and delighted in doing good to; they are <hi type="italic">the men of Judah;</hi> these he had dealt graciously with, and from them he expected suitable returns. 2. What is meant by the grapes that were expected and the wild grapes that were produces: <hi type="italic">He looked for judgment and righteousness,</hi> that the people should be honest in all their dealings and the magistrates should strictly administer justice. This might reasonably be expected among a people that had such excellent laws and rules of justice given them (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">Deut. iv. 8</reference>); but the fact was quite otherwise; instead of judgment there was the cruelty of the oppressors, and instead of righteousness the cry of the oppressed. Every thing was carried by clamour and noise, and not by equity and according to the merits of the cause. It is sad with a people when wickedness has usurped the place of judgment, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Eccl. iii. 16</reference>. It is very sad with a soul when instead of the grapes of humility, meekness, patience, love, and contempt of the world, which God looks for, there are the wild grapes of pride, passion, discontent, malice, and contempt of God—instead of the grapes of praying and praising, the wild grapes of cursing and swearing, which are a great offence to God. Some of the ancients apply this to the Jews in Christ's time, among whom God looked for righteousness (that is, that they should receive and embrace Christ), but behold a cry, that cry, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi>
entries.1dcbd448a91a37701f4393b3807b0d42c89cea57: <div eID="gen15537" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Worldly-Mindedness Reproved; The Punishment of the Sensual. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15538" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Woe unto them that join house to house, <hi type="italic">that</hi> lay field to field, till <hi type="italic">there be</hi> no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth! <hi type="super">9</hi> In mine ears <hi type="italic">said</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, Of a truth many houses shall be desolate, <hi type="italic">even</hi> great and fair, without inhabitant. <hi type="super">10</hi> Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of a homer shall yield an ephah. <hi type="super">11</hi> Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, <hi type="italic">that</hi> they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, <hi type="italic">till</hi> wine inflame them! <hi type="super">12</hi> And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , neither consider the operation of his hands. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because <hi type="italic">they have</hi> no knowledge: and their honourable men <hi type="italic">are</hi> famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the mean man shall be brought down, and the mighty man shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be humbled: <hi type="super">16</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then shall the lambs feed after their manner, and the waste places of the fat ones shall strangers eat. <div eID="gen15538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15539" type="x-p"/> The world and the flesh are the two great enemies that we are in danger of being overpowered by; yet we are in no danger if we do not ourselves yield to them. Eagerness of the world, and indulgence of the flesh, are the two sins against which the prophet, in God's name, here denounces woes. These were sins which then abounded among the men of Judah, some of the wild grapes they brought forth (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">v. 4</reference>), and for which God threatens to bring ruin upon them. They are sins which we have all need to stand upon our guard against and dread the consequences of. <div eID="gen15539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15540" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a woe to those who set their hearts upon the wealth of the world, and place their happiness in that, and increase it to themselves by indirect and unlawful means (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">v. 8</reference>), who <hi type="italic">join house to house and lay field to field, till there be no place,</hi> no room for anybody to live by them. If they could succeed, they would be placed alone in the midst of the earth, would monopolize possessions and preferments, and engross all profits and employments to themselves. Not that it is a sin for those who have a house and a field, of they have wherewithal, to purchase another; but <div eID="gen15540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15541" type="x-p"/> 1. Their fault is, (1.) That they are inordinate in their desires to enrich themselves, and make it their whole care and business to raise an estate, as if they had nothing to mind, nothing to seek, nothing to do, in this world, but that. They never know when they have enough, but the more they have the more they would have; and, like the <hi type="italic">daughters of the horseleech,</hi> they <hi type="italic">cry, Give, give.</hi> They cannot enjoy what they have, nor do good with it, but are constantly contriving and studying to make it more. They must have variety of houses, a winter-house, and a summer-house, and if another man's house or field lie convenient to theirs, as Naboth's vineyard to Ahab's, they must have that too, or they cannot be easy. (2.) That they are herein careless of others, nay, and injurious to them. They would live so as to let nobody live but themselves. So that their insatiable covetings may be gratified, they care not what becomes of all about them, what encroachments they make upon their neighbours' rights, what hardships they put upon those that they have power over or advantage against, nor what base and wicked arts they use to heap up treasure to themselves. They would swell so big as to fill all space, and yet are still unsatisfied (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Eccl. v. 10</reference>), as Alexander, who, when he fancied he had conquered the world, wept because he had not another world to conquer. <hi type="italic">Deficiente terrâ, non impletur avaritia—If the whole earth were monopolized, avarice would thirst for more.</hi> What! <hi type="italic">will you be placed alone in the midst of the earth?</hi> (so some read it); will you be so foolish as to desire it, when we have so much need of the service of others and so much comfort in their society? Will you be so foolish as to expect that the <hi type="italic">earth shall be forsaken for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job xviii. 4</reference>), when it is by multitudes that the earth is to be replenished? <hi type="italic">An propter vos solos tanta terra creata est?—Was the wide world created merely for you?</hi> Lyra. <div eID="gen15541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15542" type="x-p"/> 2. That which is threatened as the punishment of this sin is that neither the houses nor the fields they were thus greedy of should turn to any account, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9-Isa.5.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. God whispered it to the prophet in his ear, as he speaks in a like case (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">ch. xxii. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">It was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts</hi> (as God told Samuel a thing <hi type="italic">in his ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1 Sam. ix. 15</reference>); he thought he heard it still sounding in his ears; but he proclaimed it, as he ought, <hi type="italic">upon the house-tops,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">Matt. x. 27</reference>. (1.) That the houses they were so fond of should be untenanted, should stand long empty, and should yield them no rent, and go out of repair: <hi type="italic">Many houses shall be desolate,</hi> the people that should dwell in them, being cut off by sword, famine, or pestilence, or carried into captivity; or trade being dead, and poverty coming upon the country like an armed man, those that had been housekeepers were forced to become lodgers, or shift for themselves elsewhere. Even great and fair houses, that would invite tenants, and (there being a scarcity of tenants) might be taken at low rates, shall stand empty without inhabitants. God created not the earth in vain; he <hi type="italic">formed it to be inhabited,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">ch. xlv. 18</reference>. But men's projects are often frustrated, and what they frame answers not the intention. We have a saying, That fools build houses for wise men to live in; but sometimes, as the event proves, they are built for no man to live in. God has many ways to empty the most populous cities. (2.) That the fields they were so fond of should be unfruitful (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ten acres of vineyard shall yield</hi> only such a quantity of grapes as will make but <hi type="italic">one bath</hi> of wine (which was about eight gallons), <hi type="italic">and the seed of a homer,</hi> a bushel's sowing of ground, shall yield but an ephah, which was the tenth part of a homer; so that through the barrenness of the ground, or the unreasonableness of the weather, they should not have more than a tenth part of their seed again. Note, Those that set their hearts upon the world will justly be disappointed in their expectations from it. <div eID="gen15542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15543" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a woe to those that dote upon the pleasures and delights of sense, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11-Isa.5.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Sensuality ruins men as certainly as worldliness and oppression. As Christ pronounces a woe against those that are rich, so also against those that laugh now and are full (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.24-Luke.6.25">Luke vi. 24, 25</reference>), and fare sumptuously, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.19">Luke xvi. 19</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15544" type="x-p"/> 1. Who the sinners are against whom this woe is denounced. (1.) They are such as are given to drink; they make their drinking their business, have their hearts upon it, and overcharge themselves with it. They rise early to follow strong drink, as husbandmen and tradesmen do to follow their employments; as if they were afraid of losing time from that which is the greatest misspending of time. Whereas commonly those that are drunken are drunken in the night, when they have despatched the business of the day, these neglect business, abandon it, and give up themselves to the service of the flesh; for they sit at their cups all day, <hi type="italic">and continue till night, till wine inflame them</hi>—inflame their lusts (chambering and wantonness follow upon rioting and drunkenness)—inflame their passions; for who but such have <hi type="italic">contentions and wounds without cause?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29-Prov.23.35">Prov. xxiii. 29-35</reference>. They make a perfect trade of drinking; nor do they seek the shelter of the night for this work of darkness, as men ashamed of it, but <hi type="italic">count it a pleasure to riot in the day-time.</hi> See <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.13">2 Pet. ii. 13</reference>. (2.) They are such as are given to mirth. They have their feasts, and they are so merrily disposed that they cannot dine or sup without music, musical instruments of all sorts, like David (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Amos vi. 5</reference>), like Solomon (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Eccl. ii. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">the harp and the viol, the tabret and pipe,</hi> must accompany the wine, that every sense may be gratified to a nicety; they <hi type="italic">take the timbrel and harp,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.12">Job xxi. 12</reference>. The use of music is lawful in itself; but when it is excessive, when we set our hearts upon it, misspend time in it, so that it crowds our spiritual and divine pleasures and draws away the heart from God, then it turns into sin for us. (3.) They are such as never give their mind to any thing that is serious: <hi type="italic">They regard not the work of the Lord;</hi> they observe not his power, wisdom, and goodness, in those creatures which they abuse and subject to vanity, nor the bounty of his providence in giving them those good things which they make the food and fuel of their lusts. God's judgments have already seized them, and they are under the tokens of his displeasure, but they regard not; they consider not the hand of God in all these things; his hand is lifted up, but they will not see, because they will not disturb themselves in their pleasures nor think what God is doing with them. <div eID="gen15544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15545" type="x-p"/> 2. What the judgments are which are denounced against them, and in part executed. It is here foretold, (1.) that they should be dislodged; the land should spue out these drunkards (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">My people</hi> (so they call themselves, and were proud of it) have therefore <hi type="italic">gone into captivity,</hi> are as sure to go as if they were gone already, <hi type="italic">because they have no knowledge;</hi> how should they have knowledge when by their excessive drinking they make sots and fools of themselves? They set up for wits; but because they regard not God's controversy with them, nor take any care to make their peace with him, they may truly be said to have no knowledge; and the reason is because they will have none; they are inconsiderate and wilful, and are therefore destroyed for lack of knowledge. (2.) That they should be impoverished, and come to want that which they had wasted and abused to excess: Even <hi type="italic">their glory are men of famine,</hi> subject to it and slain by it; and <hi type="italic">their multitude are dried up with thirst.</hi> Both the great men and the common people are ready to perish for want of bread and water. This is the effect of the failure of the corn (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">v. 10</reference>), for <hi type="italic">the king himself is served of the field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.9">Eccl. v. 9</reference>. And when the vintage fails the drunkards are called upon to weep, because <hi type="italic">the new wine is cut off from their mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">Joel i. 5</reference>), and not so much because now they want it as because when they had it they abused it. It is just with God to make men want that for necessity which they have abused to excess. (3.) What multitudes should be cut off by famine and sword (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore hell has enlarged herself.</hi> Tophet, the common burying-place, proves too little; so many are there to be buried that they shall be forced to enlarge it. The grave has opened her mouth without measure, <hi type="italic">never saying, It is enough,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15-Prov.30.16">Prov. xxx. 15, 16</reference>. It may be understood of the place of the damned; luxury and sensuality fill these regions of darkness and horror; there those are tormented who made a god of their belly, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Phil. iii. 19</reference>. (4.) That they should be humbled and abased, and all their honours laid in the dust. This will be done effectually by death and the grave: <hi type="italic">Their glory shall descend,</hi> not only to the earth, but into it; it shall not <hi type="italic">descend after them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Ps. xlix. 17</reference>), to stand them in any stead on the other side death, but it shall die and be buried with them—poor glory, which will thus wither! Did they glory in their numbers? Their multitude shall go down to the pit, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Ezek. xxxi. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.32">xxxii. 32</reference>. Did they glory in the figure they made? Their pomp shall be at an end; their shouts with which they triumphed, and were attended. Did they glory in their mirth? Death will turn it into mourning; he that rejoices and revels, and never knows what it is to be serious, shall go thither where there are weeping and wailing. Thus the mean man and the mighty man meet together in the grave and under mortifying judgments. Let a man be ever so high, death will bring him low—ever so mean, death will bring him lower, in the prospect of which the eyes of the lofty should now be humbled, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.15">v. 15</reference>. It becomes those to look low that must shortly be laid low. <div eID="gen15545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15546" type="x-p"/> 3. What the fruit of these judgments shall be. <div eID="gen15546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> (1.) God shall be glorified, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.16">v. 16</reference>. He that is the Lord of hosts, and the holy God, shall be exalted and sanctified in the judgment and righteousness of these dispensations. His justice must be owned in bringing those low what exalted themselves; and herein he is glorified, [1.] As a God is irresistible power. He will herein be exalted as the Lord of hosts, that is able to break the strongest, humble the proudest, and tame the most unruly. Power is not exalted but in judgment. It is the honour of God that, though he has a mighty arm, yet <hi type="italic">judgment and justice are</hi> always <hi type="italic">the habitation of his throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.13-Ps.89.14">Ps. lxxxix. 13, 14</reference>. [2.] As a God of unspotted purity. He that is holy, infinitely holy, shall be sanctified (that is, shall be owned and declared to be holy) in the righteous punishment of proud men. Note, When proud men are humbled the great God is honoured, and ought to be honoured by us. <div eID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> (2.) Good people shall be relieved and succoured (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall the lambs feed after their manner;</hi> the meek ones of the earth, who followed the Lamb, who were persecuted, and put into fear by those proud oppressors, shall feed quietly, feed in the green pastures, and there shall be none to make them afraid. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">Ezek. xxxiv. 14</reference>. When the enemies of the church are cut off then have the churches rest. <hi type="italic">They shall feed at their pleasure;</hi> so some read it. <hi type="italic">Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth,</hi> and delight themselves in abundant peace. <hi type="italic">They shall feed according to their order or capacity</hi> (so others read it), as they are able to hear the word, that bread of life. <div eID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> (3.) The country shall be laid waste, and become a prey to the neighbours: <hi type="italic">The waste places of the fats ones,</hi> the possessions of those rich men that lived at their ease, shall be eaten by strangers that were nothing akin to them. In the captivity the poor of the land were left for <hi type="italic">vine-dressers and husbandmen</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">2 Kings xxv. 12</reference>); these were the lambs that fed in the pastures of the fats ones, which were laid in common for strangers to eat. When the church of the Jews, those fat ones, was laid waste, their privileges were transferred to the Gentiles, who had been long strangers, and the lambs of Christ's flock were welcome to them.
entries.9cb395c5172cbb50d0ef03cfbcd24f703e2dd7f8: <div eID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Denunciations against Sin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope: <hi type="super">19</hi> That say, Let him make speed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hasten his work, that we may see <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know <hi type="italic">it!</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! <hi type="super">21</hi> Woe unto <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight! <hi type="super">22</hi> Woe unto <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink: <hi type="super">23</hi> Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him! <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, <hi type="italic">so</hi> their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">25</hi> Therefore is the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> kindled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble, and their carcases <hi type="italic">were</hi> torn in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out still. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly: <hi type="super">27</hi> None shall be weary nor stumble among them; none shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken: <hi type="super">28</hi> Whose arrows <hi type="italic">are</hi> sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind: <hi type="super">29</hi> Their roaring <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> like a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry <hi type="italic">it</hi> away safe, and none shall deliver <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">30</hi> And in that day they shall roar against them like the roaring of the sea: and if <hi type="italic">one</hi> look unto the land, behold darkness <hi type="italic">and</hi> sorrow, and the light is darkened in the heavens thereof. <div eID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> Here are, I. Sins described which will bring judgments upon a people: and this perhaps is not only a charge drawn up against the men of Judah who lived at that time, and the particular articles of that charge, though it may relate primarily to them, but is rather intended for warning to all people, in all ages, to take heed of these sins, as destructive both to particular persons and to communities, and exposing men to God's wrath and his righteous judgments. Those are here said to be in a woeful condition, <div eID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> 1. Who are eagerly set upon sin, and violent in their sinful pursuits (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.18">v. 18</reference>), who <hi type="italic">draw iniquity with cords of vanity,</hi> who take as much pains to sin as the cattle do that draw a team, who put themselves to the stretch for the gratifying of their inordinate appetites, and, to humour a base lust, offer violence to nature itself. They think themselves as sure of compassing their wicked project as if they were pulling it towards them with strong cart-ropes; but they will find themselves disappointed, for they will prove cords of vanity, which will break when they come to any stress. For <hi type="italic">the righteous Lord will cut in sunder the cords of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.129.4">Ps. cxxix. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job iv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Prov. xxii. 8</reference>. They are by long custom and confirmed habits so hardened in sin that they cannot get clear of it. Those that sin through infirmity are drawn away by sin; those that sin presumptuously draw iniquity to them, in spite of the oppositions of Providence and the checks of conscience. Some by sin understand the punishment of sin: they pull God's judgments upon their own heads as it were, with cart-ropes. <div eID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> 2. Who set the justice of God at defiance, and challenge the Almighty to do his worst (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">They say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work;</hi> this is the same language with that of the scoffers of the last days, who say, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> and therefore it is that, like them, they <hi type="italic">draw iniquity with cords of vanity,</hi> are violent and daring in sin, and walk after their own lusts, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3-2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 3, 4</reference>. (1.) They ridicule the prophets, and banter them. It is in scorn that they call God <hi type="italic">the Holy One of Israel,</hi> because the prophets used with great veneration to call him so. (2.) They will not believe the revelation of God's wrath from heaven against their ungodliness and unrighteousness; unless they see it executed, they will not know it, as if the curse were <hi type="italic">brutum fulmen—a mere flash,</hi> and all the threatenings of the word bugbears to frighten fools and children. (3.) If God should appear against them, as he has threatened, yet they think themselves able to make their part good with him, and provoke him to jealousy, as if they were stronger than he, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.22">1 Cor. x. 22</reference>. "We have heard his word, but it is all talk; let him hasten his work, we shall shift for ourselves well enough." Note, Those that wilfully persist in sin consider not the power of God's anger. <div eID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> 3. Who confound and overthrow the distinctions between moral good and evil, <hi type="italic">who call evil good and moral evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">v. 20</reference>), who not only live in the omission of that which is good, but condemn it, argue against it, and, because they will not practise it themselves, run it down in others, and fasten invidious epithets upon it—not only do that which is evil, but justify it, and applaud it, and recommend it to others as safe and good. Note, (1.) Virtue and piety are good, for they are light and sweet, they are pleasant and right; but sin and wickedness are evil; they are darkness, all the fruit of ignorance and mistake, and will be bitterness in the latter end. (2.) Those do a great deal of wrong to God, and religion, and conscience, to their own souls, and to the souls of others, who misrepresent these, and put false colours upon them—who call drunkenness good fellowship, and covetousness good husbandry, and, when they persecute the people of God, think they do him good service—and, on the other hand, who call seriousness ill-nature, and sober singularity ill-breeding, who say all manner of evil falsely concerning the ways of godliness, and do what they can to form in men's minds prejudices against them, and this in defiance of evidence as plain and convincing as that of sense, by which we distinguish, beyond contradiction, between light and darkness, and between that which to the taste is sweet and that which is bitter. <div eID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> 4. Who though they are guilty of such gross mistakes as these have a great opinion of their own judgments, and value themselves mightily upon their understanding (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.21">v. 21</reference>): They are <hi type="italic">wise in their own eyes;</hi> they think themselves able to disprove and baffle the reproofs and convictions of God's word, and to evade and elude both the searches and the reaches of his judgments; they think they can outwit Infinite Wisdom and countermine Providence itself. Or it may be taken more generally: God resists the proud, those particularly who are conceited of their own wisdom and lean to their own understanding; such must become fools, that they may be truly wise, or else, at their end they shall appear to be fools before all the world. <div eID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15556" type="x-p"/> 5. Who glory in it as a great accomplishment that they are able to bear a great deal of strong liquor without being overcome by it (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">who are mighty to drink wine,</hi> and use their strength and vigour, not in the service of their country, but in the service of their lusts. Let drunkards know from this scripture that, (1.) They ungratefully abuse their bodily strength, which God has given them for good purposes, and by degrees cannot but weaken it. (2.) It will not excuse them from the guilt of drunkenness that they can drink hard and yet keep their feet. (3.) Those who boast of their drinking down others glory in their shame. (4.) How light soever men make of their drunkenness, it is a sin which will certainly lay them open to the wrath and curse of God. <div eID="gen15556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> 6. Who, as judges, pervert justice, and go counter to all rules of equity, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">v. 23</reference>. This follows upon the former; they <hi type="italic">drink and forget the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 5</reference>), and <hi type="italic">err through wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">ch. xxviii. 7</reference>), and take bribes, that they may have wherewithal to maintain their luxury. They <hi type="italic">justify the wicked for reward,</hi> and find some pretence or other to clear him from his guilt and shelter him from punishment; and they condemn the innocent, and <hi type="italic">take away their righteousness from them,</hi> that is, overrule their pleas, deprive them of the means of clearing up their innocency, and give judgment against them. In causes between man and man, might and money would at any time prevail against right and justice; and he who was ever so plainly in the wrong would with a small bribe carry the cause and recover the costs. In criminal causes, though the prisoner ever so plainly appeared to be guilty, yet for a reward they would acquit him; if he were innocent, yet if he did not fee them well, nay, if they were feed by the malicious prosecutor, or if they themselves had spleen against him, they would condemn him. <div eID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15558" type="x-p"/> II. The judgments described, which these sins would bring upon them. Let not those expect to live easily who live thus wickedly; for the righteous God will take vengeance, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24-Isa.5.30">v. 24-30</reference>. Here we may observe, <div eID="gen15558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> 1. How complete this ruin will be, and how necessarily and unavoidably it will follow upon their sins. He had compared this people to a vine (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">v. 7</reference>), well fixed, and which, it was hoped, would be flourishing and fruitful; but the grace of God towards it was received in vain, and then the root became rottenness, being dried up from beneath, and the blossom would of course blow off as dust, as a light and worthless thing, <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job xviii. 16</reference>. Sin weakens the strength, the root, of a people, so that they are easily rooted up; it defaces the beauty, the blossoms, of a people, and takes away the hopes of fruit. The sin of unfruitfulness is punished with the plague of unfruitfulness. Sinners make themselves as stubble and chaff, combustible matter, proper fuel to the fire of God's wrath, which then of course devours and consumes them, <hi type="italic">as the fire devours the stubble,</hi> and nobody can hinder it, or cares to hinder it. Chaff is consumed, unhelped and unpitied. <div eID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> 2. How just the ruin will be: <hi type="italic">Because they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts,</hi> and would not have him to reign over them; and, as the law of Moses was rejected and thrown off, so <hi type="italic">the word of the Holy One of Israel</hi> by his servants the prophets, putting them in mind of his law and calling them to obedience, was despised and disregarded. God does not reject men for every transgression of his law and word; but, when his word is despised and his law cast away, what can they expect but that God should utterly abandon them? <div eID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> 3. Whence this ruin should come (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">v. 25</reference>): it is destruction from the Almighty. (1.) The justice of God appoints it; for that is <hi type="italic">the anger of the Lord</hi> which is <hi type="italic">kindled against his people,</hi> his necessary vindication of the honour of his holiness and authority. (2.) The power of God effects it: <hi type="italic">He has stretched forth his hand against them.</hi> That hand which had many a time been stretched out for them against their enemies is now stretched out against them at full length and in its full vigour; and <hi type="italic">who knows the power of his anger?</hi> Whether they are sensible of it or no, it is God that has smitten them, has blasted their vine and made it wither. <div eID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> 4. The consequences and continuance of this ruin. When God comes forth in wrath against a people the hills tremble, fear seizes even their great men, who are strong and high, the earth shakes under men and is ready to sink; and as this feels dreadful (what does more so than an earthquake?) so what sight can be more frightful than the carcases of men torn with dogs, or thrown <hi type="italic">as dung</hi> (so the margin reads it) <hi type="italic">in the midst of the streets?</hi> This intimates that great multitudes should be slain, not only soldiers in the field of battle, but the inhabitants of their cities put to the sword in cold blood, and that the survivors should neither have hands nor hearts to bury them. This is very dreadful, and yet such is the merit of sin that, <hi type="italic">for all this, God's anger is not turned away;</hi> that fire will burn as long as there remains any of the stubble and chaff to be fuel for it; <hi type="italic">and his hand,</hi> which he stretched forth against his people to smite them, because they do not by prayer take hold of it, nor by reformation submit themselves to it, <hi type="italic">is stretched out still.</hi> <div eID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> 5. The instruments that should be employed in bringing this ruin upon them: it should be done by the incursions of a foreign enemy, that should lay all waste. No particular enemy is named, and therefore we are to take it as a prediction of all the several judgments of this kind which God brought upon the Jews, Sennacherib's invasion soon after, and the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans first and at last by the Romans; and I think it is to be looked upon also as a threatening of the like desolation of those countries which harbour and countenance those sins mentioned in the foregoing verses; it is an exposition of those woes. When God designs the ruin of a provoking people, <div eID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> (1.) He can send a great way off for instruments to be employed in effecting it; he can raise forces from afar, and summon them from the end of the earth to attend his service, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">v. 26</reference>. Those who know him not are made use of to fulfil his counsel, when, by reason of their distance, they can scarcely be supposed to have any ends of their own to serve. If God set up his standard, he can incline men's hearts to enlist themselves under it, though perhaps they know not why or wherefore. When the Lord of hosts is pleased to make a general muster of the forces he has at his command, he has a great army in an instant, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joel ii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">11</reference>. He needs not sound a trumpet, nor beat a drum, to give them notice or to animate them; no, he does but hiss to them, or rather whistle to them, and that is enough; they hear that, and that puts courage into them. Note, God has all the creatures at his beck. <div eID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> (2.) He can make them come into the service with incredible expedition: <hi type="italic">Behold, they shall come with speed swiftly.</hi> Note, [1.] Those who will do God's work must not loiter, must not linger, nor shall they when his time has come. [2.] Those who defy God's judgments will be ashamed of their insolence when it is too late; they said scornfully (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let him make speed, let him hasten his work,</hi> and they shall find, to their terror and confusion, that he will; <hi type="italic">in one hour has the judgment come.</hi> <div eID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15566" type="x-p"/> (3.) He can carry them on in the service with amazing forwardness and fury. This is described here in very elegant and lofty expressions, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27-Isa.5.30">v. 27-30</reference>. [1.] Though their marches be very long, yet <hi type="italic">none among them shall be weary;</hi> so desirous they be to engage that they shall forget their weariness, and make no complaints of it. [2.] Though the way be rough, and perhaps embarrassed by the usual policies of war, yet none among them shall <hi type="italic">stumble,</hi> but all the difficulties in their way shall easily be got over. [3.] Though they be forced to keep constant watch, yet <hi type="italic">none shall slumber nor sleep,</hi> so intent shall they be upon their work, in prospect of having the plunder of the city for their pains. [4.] They shall not desire any rest of relaxation; they shall not put off their clothes, nor <hi type="italic">loose the girdle of their loins,</hi> but shall always have their belts on and swords by their sides. [5.] They shall not meet with the least hindrance to retard their march or oblige them to halt; not a <hi type="italic">latchet of their shoes shall be broken</hi> which they must stay to mend, as <reference osisRef="Josh.9.13">Josh. ix. 13</reference>. [6.] Their arms and ammunition shall all be fixed, and in good posture; <hi type="italic">their arrows sharp,</hi> to wound deep, <hi type="italic">and all their bows bent,</hi> none unstrung, for they expect to be soon in action. [7.] Their horses and chariots of war shall all be fit for service; their horses so strong, so hardy, that <hi type="italic">their hoofs shall be like flint,</hi> far from being beaten, or made tender, by their long march; and the wheels of their chariots not broken, or battered, or out of repair, but swift <hi type="italic">like a whirlwind,</hi> turning round so strongly upon their axle-trees. [8.] All the soldiers shall be bold and daring (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their roaring,</hi> or shouting, before a battle, <hi type="italic">shall be like a lion,</hi> who with his roaring animates himself, and terrifies all about him. Those who would not hear the voice of God speaking to them by his prophets, but stopped their ears against their charms, shall be made to hear the voice of their enemies roaring against them and shall not be able to turn a deaf ear to it. <hi type="italic">They shall roar like the roaring of the sea</hi> in a storm; it roars and threatens to swallow up, as the lion roars and threatens to tear in pieces. [9.] There shall not be the least prospect of relief or succour. The enemy shall come in like a flood, and there shall be none to lift up a standard against him. He shall seize the prey, and none shall deliver it, none shall be able to deliver it, nay, none shall so much as dare to attempt the deliverance of it, but shall give it up for lost. Let the distressed look which way they will, every thing appears dismal; for, if God frowns upon us, how can any creature smile? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Look round to the earth, to the land, to that land that used to be the land of light and the joy of the whole earth, and <hi type="italic">behold darkness and sorrow,</hi> all frightful, all mournful, nothing hopeful. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Look up to heaven, and there the light is darkened, where one would expect to have found it. If the light is darkened in the heavens, how great is that darkness! If God hide his face, no marvel the heavens hide theirs and appear gloomy, <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>. It is our wisdom, by keeping a good conscience, to keep all clear between us and heaven, that we may have light from above even when clouds and darkness are round about us.  <chapter eID="Isa.5"/> <div eID="gen15566" type="x-p"/>

entries.d2f06cfb5a62ecdc291bf09a1252eeeed1e2ae11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8389"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.30">Is 5:1-30</reference>. Parable of Jehovah's Vineyard.</title> <div sID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> A new prophecy; entire in itself. Probably delivered about the same time as the second and third chapters, in Uzziah's reign. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.15">Is 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.16">16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">Is 2:17</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Is 3:14</reference>. However, the close of the chapter alludes generally to the still distant invasion of Assyrians in a later reign (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Is 7:18</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Is 5:25</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">Is 9:12</reference>). When the time drew nigh, according to the ordinary prophetic usage, he handles the details more particularly (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.8.22">Is 7:1-8:22</reference>); namely, the calamities caused by the Syro-Israelitish invasion, and subsequently by the Assyrians whom Ahaz had invited to his help.<div eID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8389"/><hi type="bold">1. to--</hi>rather, "concerning" [Gesenius], that is, in the person of My beloved, as His representative [Vitringa]. Isaiah gives a hint of the distinction and yet unity of the Divine Persons (compare He with I, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of my beloved--</hi>inspired by Him; or else, a tender song [Castalio]. By a slight change of reading "a song of His love" [Houbigant]. "The Beloved" is Jehovah, the Second Person, the "Angel" of God the Father, not in His character as incarnate Messiah, but as God of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.20">Ex 23:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">32:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">33:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vineyard--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Is 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">Psa 80:8</reference>, &c.). The Jewish covenant-people, separated from the nations for His glory, as the object of His peculiar care (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.1">Mt 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.33">21:33</reference>). Jesus Christ in the "vineyard" of the New Testament Church is the same as the Old Testament Angel of the Jewish covenant.<div eID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruitful hill--</hi>literally, "a horn" ("peak," as the Swiss shreckhorn) of the son of oil; poetically, for very fruitful. Suggestive of isolation, security, and a sunny aspect. Isaiah alludes plainly to the Song of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Song.6.3">So 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.11">8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.8.12">12</reference>), in the words "His vineyard" and "my Beloved" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">61:10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>). The transition from "branch" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>) to "vineyard" here is not unnatural. <div eID="gen13458" type="x-p"/>
entries.86bac1cc9a54cc126eb70c9a17d6dfeab00783f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8390"/><div sID="gen13459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8390"/><hi type="bold">2. fenced--</hi>rather, "digged and trenched" the ground to prepare it for planting the vines [Maurer].<div eID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choicest vine--</hi>Hebrew, sorek; called still in Morocco, serki; the grapes had scarcely perceptible seeds; the Persian kishmish or bedana, that is, "without seed" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Ge 49:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower--</hi>to watch the vineyard against the depredations of man or beast, and for the use of the owner (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.33">Mt 21:33</reference>).<div eID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wine-press--</hi>including the wine-fat; both hewn, for coolness, out of the rocky undersoil of the vineyard.<div eID="gen13462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild grapes--</hi>The Hebrew expresses offensive putrefaction, answering to the corrupt state of the Jews. Fetid fruit of the wild vine [Maurer], instead of "choicest" grapes. Of the poisonous monk's hood [Gesenius]. The Arabs call the fruit of the nightshade "wolf grapes" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.39-2Kgs.4.41">2Ki 4:39-41</reference>). Jerome tries to specify the details of the parable; the "fence," angels; the "stones gathered out," idols; the "tower," the "temple in the midst" of Judea; the "wine-press," the altar. <div eID="gen13463" type="x-p"/>
entries.e84af3d1463ce4c875eaa8f0d7bdaa437e1b1e92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8391"/><div sID="gen13464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8391"/><hi type="bold">3. And now, &c.--</hi>appeal of God to themselves, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Is 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mi 6:3</reference>. So Jesus Christ, in <reference osisRef="Matt.21.40">Mt 21:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.41">41</reference>, alluding in the very form of expression to this, makes them pass sentence on themselves. God condemns sinners "out of their own mouth" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.6">De 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.6">Job 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.22">Lu 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13464" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac191be21feb7f396d84be805063c4ffd5d601a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8392"/><div sID="gen13465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8392"/>4. God has done all that could be done for the salvation of sinners, consistently with His justice and goodness. The God of nature is, as it were, amazed at the unnatural fruit of so well-cared a vineyard. <div eID="gen13465" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cc0ce032978a72e16af13dcc780ddb35a071b90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8393"/><div sID="gen13466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8393"/><hi type="bold">5. go to--</hi>that is, attend to me.<div eID="gen13466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hedge ... wall--</hi>It had both; a proof of the care of the owner. But now it shall be trodden down by wild beasts (enemies) (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.12">Psa 80:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen13467" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d7a9f4885d7d97137985e778148655a42674583: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8394"/><div sID="gen13468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8394"/><hi type="bold">6. I will ... command--</hi>The parable is partly dropped and Jehovah, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">Is 5:7</reference>, is implied to be the Owner: for He alone, not an ordinary husbandman (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Mt 21:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Lu 17:22</reference>), could give such a "command."<div eID="gen13468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no rain--</hi>antitypically, the heaven-sent teachings of the prophets (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.11">Am 8:11</reference>). Not accomplished in the Babylonish captivity; for Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied during or after it. But in gospel times. <div eID="gen13469" type="x-p"/>
entries.03753ca649c13207439107edd6d85cf0dc5f050b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8395"/><div sID="gen13470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8395"/>7. Isaiah here applies the parable. It is no mere human owner, nor a literal vineyard that is meant.<div eID="gen13470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vineyard of the Lord--</hi>His only one (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant--</hi>"the plant of his delight"; just as the husbandman was at pains to select the sorek, or "choicest vine" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>); so God's election of the Jews.<div eID="gen13472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>justice. The play upon words is striking in the Hebrew, He looked for mishpat, but behold mispat ("bloodshed"); for tsedaqua, but behold tseaqua (the cry that attends anarchy, covetousness, and dissipation, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">11, 12</reference>; compare the cry of the rabble by which justice was overborne in the case of Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.23">Mt 27:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen13473" type="x-p"/>
entries.bad2c44fea8e17ef13c3f25e9e6de9b970cac8dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8396"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.5.8-Isa.5.23">Is 5:8-23</reference>. Six Distinct Woes against Crimes.</title> <div sID="gen13474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8396"/>8. (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.13">Le 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.2">Mi 2:2</reference>). The jubilee restoration of possessions was intended as a guard against avarice.<div eID="gen13474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till there be no place--</hi>left for any one else.<div eID="gen13475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may be--</hi>rather, and ye be.<div eID="gen13476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the earth--</hi>the land. <div eID="gen13477" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0a5d0e49722c23dbb8182b220aec0abed584022: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8397"/><div sID="gen13478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8397"/><hi type="bold">9. In mine ears ... the Lord--</hi>namely, has revealed it, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Is 22:14</reference>.<div eID="gen13478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desolate--</hi>literally, "a desolation," namely, on account of the national sins.<div eID="gen13479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great and fair--</hi>houses. <div eID="gen13480" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f07d95725d5a3aabe8172133d08684f69f92d29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8398"/><div sID="gen13481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8398"/><hi type="bold">10. acres--</hi>literally, "yokes"; as much as one yoke of oxen could plow in a day.<div eID="gen13481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one--</hi>only.<div eID="gen13482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bath--</hi>of wine; seven and a half gallons.<div eID="gen13483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">homer ... ephah--</hi>Eight bushels of seed would yield only three pecks of produce (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.11">Eze 45:11</reference>). The ephah and bath, one-tenth of an homer. <div eID="gen13484" type="x-p"/>
entries.839fdee56cda73e0f7daee763cf5b7b392257b2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8399"/><div sID="gen13485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8399"/><hi type="bold">11. Second Woe--</hi>against intemperance.<div eID="gen13485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">early--</hi>when it was regarded especially shameful to drink (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.15">Ac 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.7">1Th 5:7</reference>). Banquets for revelry began earlier than usual (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ec 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen13486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong drink--</hi>Hebrew, sichar, implying intoxication.<div eID="gen13487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continue--</hi>drinking all day till evening. <div eID="gen13488" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cc10dd8eabd57d5ba9dda13300296d168efb5c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8400"/><div sID="gen13489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8400"/>12. Music was common at ancient feasts (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.8">Is 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Am 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen13489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">viol--</hi>an instrument with twelve strings [Josephus, Antiquities, 8.10].<div eID="gen13490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabret--</hi>Hebrew, toph, from the use of which in drowning the cries of children sacrificed to Moloch, Tophet received its name. Arabic, duf. A kettle drum, or tambourine.<div eID="gen13491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pipe--</hi>flute or flageolet: from a Hebrew root "to bore through"; or else, "to dance" (compare <reference osisRef="Job.21.11-Job.21.15">Job 21:11-15</reference>).<div eID="gen13492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">regard not ... Lord--</hi>a frequent effect of feasting (<reference osisRef="Job.1.5">Job 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>).<div eID="gen13493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work ... operation--</hi>in punishing the guilty (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Is 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Is 10:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13494" type="x-p"/>
entries.a960308a55397f065a687d41a4513fe6ca8c088e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8401"/><div sID="gen13495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8401"/><hi type="bold">13. are gone--</hi>The prophet sees the future as if it were before his eyes.<div eID="gen13495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no knowledge--</hi>because of their foolish recklessness (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Is 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.6">Ho 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.44">Lu 19:44</reference>).<div eID="gen13496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">famished--</hi>awful contrast to their luxurious feasts (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen13497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">multitude--</hi>plebeians in contradistinction to the "honorable men," or nobles.<div eID="gen13498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thirst--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.107.4">Psa 107:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">5</reference>). Contrast to their drinking (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>). In their deportation and exile, they shall hunger and thirst. <div eID="gen13499" type="x-p"/>
entries.02aca94f8303eb6313c88b366e44b0bee01b10cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8402"/><div sID="gen13500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8402"/><hi type="bold">14. hell--</hi>the grave; Hebrew, sheol; Greek, hades; "the unseen world of spirits." Not here, "the place of torment." Poetically, it is represented as enlarging itself immensely, in order to receive the countless hosts of Jews, which should perish (<reference osisRef="Num.16.30">Nu 16:30</reference>).<div eID="gen13500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their--</hi>that is, of the Jewish people.<div eID="gen13501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that rejoiceth--</hi>the drunken reveller in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen13502" type="x-p"/>
entries.799d02b4f6525b68332f70883fe28fc2bacd0833: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8403"/><div sID="gen13503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8403"/>15. (Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">Is 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.17">11, 17</reference>). All ranks, "mean" and "mighty" alike; so "honorable" and "multitude" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Is 5:13</reference>). <div eID="gen13503" type="x-p"/>
entries.54c151fad421a91883816e3f2f7a774d914ff3e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8404"/><div sID="gen13504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8404"/>16. God shall be "exalted" in man's view, because of His manifestation of His "justice" in punishing the guilty.<div eID="gen13504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctified--</hi>regarded as holy by reason of His "righteous" dealings. <div eID="gen13505" type="x-p"/>
entries.578a371c3dec91ee6874b8445d9c89bc9d8f3996: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8405"/><div sID="gen13506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8405"/><hi type="bold">17. after their manner--</hi>literally, "according to their own word," that is, at will. Otherwise, as in their own pasture [Gesenius]: so the Hebrew in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mi 2:12</reference>. The lands of the Scenite tent dwellers (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.7">Jr 35:7</reference>). Arab shepherds in the neighborhood shall roam at large, the whole of Judea being so desolate as to become a vast pasturage.<div eID="gen13506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waste ... fat ones--</hi>the deserted lands of the rich ("fat," <reference osisRef="Ps.22.29">Psa 22:29</reference>), then gone into captivity; "strangers," that is, nomad tribes shall make their flocks to feed on [Maurer]. Figuratively, "the lambs" are the pious, "the fat ones" the impious. So tender disciples of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.21.15">Joh 21:15</reference>) are called "lambs"; being meek, harmless, poor, and persecuted. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.18">Eze 39:18</reference>, where the fatlings are the rich and great (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">1Co 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">27</reference>). The "strangers" are in this view the "other sheep not of the" the Jewish "fold" (<reference osisRef="John.10.16">Joh 10:16</reference>), the Gentiles whom Jesus Christ shall "bring" to be partakers of the rich privileges (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Ro 11:17</reference>) which the Jews ("fat ones," Eze 34. 16) fell from. Thus "after their (own) manner" will express that the Christian Church should worship God in freedom, released from legal bondage (<reference osisRef="John.4.23">Joh 4:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Ga 5:1</reference>). <div eID="gen13507" type="x-p"/>
entries.92e4c741988531e516041df4e6e83cc7ec6ccb2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8406"/><div sID="gen13508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8406"/><hi type="bold">18. Third Woe--</hi>against obstinate perseverance in sin, as if they wished to provoke divine judgments.<div eID="gen13508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity--</hi>guilt, incurring punishment [Maurer].<div eID="gen13509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cords, &c.--</hi>cart-rope--Rabbins say, "An evil inclination is at first like a fine hair-string, but the finishing like a cart-rope." The antithesis is between the slender cords of sophistry, like the spider's web (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Is 59:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.14">Job 8:14</reference>), with which one sin draws on another, until they at last bind themselves with great guilt as with a cart-rope. They strain every nerve in sin.<div eID="gen13510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanity--</hi>wickedness.<div eID="gen13511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin--</hi>substantive, not a verb: they draw on themselves "sin" and its penalty recklessly. <div eID="gen13512" type="x-p"/>
entries.524a139731021536b939dfa5843a2eaf363b6e8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8407"/><div sID="gen13513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8407"/><hi type="bold">19. work--</hi>vengeance (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Is 5:12</reference>). Language of defiance to God.
