So Lamech's boast of impunity (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.23">Ge 4:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.24">24</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.17.15">Jr 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen13513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsel--</hi>God's threatened purpose to punish. <div eID="gen13514" type="x-p"/>
entries.297392eb449f17df5161aca3a3650d772e4998bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8408"/><div sID="gen13515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8408"/><hi type="bold">20. Fourth Woe--</hi>against those who confound the distinctions of right and wrong (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>), "reprobate," Greek, "undiscriminating: the moral perception darkened."<div eID="gen13515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bitter ... sweet--</hi>sin is bitter (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.23">Ac 8:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>); though it seem sweet for a time (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.17">Pr 9:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">18</reference>). Religion is sweet (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">Psa 119:103</reference>). <div eID="gen13516" type="x-p"/>
entries.f60c88b6ba2a1c9526d337dd625f60e3f3f0f68c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8409"/><div sID="gen13517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8409"/><hi type="bold">21. Fifth Woe--</hi>against those who were so "wise in their own eyes" as to think they knew better than the prophet, and therefore rejected his warnings (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Is 29:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen13517" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f84d1423502616780915f867e76ae0c480a9e62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8410"/><div sID="gen13518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8410"/><hi type="bold">22-23. Sixth Woe--</hi>against corrupt judges, who, "mighty" in drinking "wine" (a boast still not uncommon), if not in defending their country, obtain the means of self-indulgence by taking bribes ("reward"). The two verses are closely joined [Maurer].<div eID="gen13518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mingle strong drink--</hi>not with water, but spices to make it intoxicating (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.2">Pr 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take away the righteousness--</hi>set aside the just claims of those having a righteous cause. <div eID="gen13520" type="x-p"/>
entries.88529a583b7b15930c26b2203d0cb13fa9bf8e50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8411"/><div sID="gen13521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8411"/>24. Literally, "tongue of fire eateth" (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.3">Ac 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flame consumeth the chaff--</hi>rather, withered grass falleth before the flame (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen13522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">root ... blossom--</hi>entire decay, both the hidden source and outward manifestations of prosperity, perishing (<reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>; Mal 4:1).<div eID="gen13523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast away ... law--</hi>in its spirit, while retaining the letter. <div eID="gen13524" type="x-p"/>
entries.464236c745898188a418a9a2253837b7034cea1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8412"/><div sID="gen13525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8412"/><hi type="bold">25. anger ... kindled--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.13">2Ki 22:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen13525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hills ... tremble--</hi>This probably fixes the date of this chapter, as it refers to the earthquake in the days of Uzziah (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zec 14:5</reference>). The earth trembled as if conscious of the presence of God (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.24">Jr 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Ha 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">torn--</hi>rather, were as dung (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>).<div eID="gen13527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For all this, &c.--</hi>This burden of the prophet's strains, with dirge-like monotony, is repeated at <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">Is 9:12</reference>, 17, 21; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">10:4</reference>. With all the past calamities, still heavier judgments are impending; which he specifies in the rest of the chapter (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.14">Le 26:14</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen13528" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c26658d6830060583a159296bedad253e8d00d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8413"/><div sID="gen13529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8413"/><hi type="bold">26. lift ... ensign--</hi>to call together the hostile nations to execute His judgments on Judea (Is 10:5-7; 45:<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1">1</reference>). But for mercy to it, in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">18:3</reference>.<div eID="gen13529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hiss--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Is 7:18</reference>). Bees were drawn out of their hives by the sound of a flute, or hissing, or whistling (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8">Zec 10:8</reference>). God will collect the nations round Judea like bees (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.44">De 1:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>).<div eID="gen13530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end of the earth--</hi>the widely distant subject races of which the Assyrian army was made up (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>). The ulterior fulfilment took place in the siege under Roman Titus. Compare "end of the earth" (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">De 28:49</reference>, &c.). So the pronoun is singular in the Hebrew, for "them," "their," "whose" (him, his, &c.), <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26-Isa.5.29">Is 5:26-29</reference>; referring to some particular nation and person [Horsley]. <div eID="gen13531" type="x-p"/>
entries.3671096f142e931e83119dc81bc9928df24c6eb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8414"/><div sID="gen13532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8414"/><hi type="bold">27. weary--</hi>with long marches (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.18">De 25:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... slumber--</hi>requiring no rest.<div eID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">girdle--</hi>with which the ancient loose robes used to be girded for action. Ever ready for march or battle.<div eID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor the latchet ... broken--</hi>The soles were attached to the feet, not by upper leather as with us, but by straps. So securely clad that not even a strap of their sandals gives way, so as to impede their march. <div eID="gen13535" type="x-p"/>
entries.357fe0bab0cb8ab7c0b43ba1cf20a3ae25d97392: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8415"/><div sID="gen13536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8415"/><hi type="bold">28. bent--</hi>ready for battle.<div eID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hoofs ... flint--</hi>The ancients did not shoe their horses: hence the value of hard hoofs for long marches.<div eID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>of their chariots. The Assyrian army abounded in cavalry and chariots (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.8">36:8</reference>). <div eID="gen13538" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd34a8031595ede6e47b3db4c9926a3febb8ad8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8416"/><div sID="gen13539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8416"/><hi type="bold">29. roaring--</hi>their battle cry. <div eID="gen13539" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa90a5fa029b35c3e36cf48eb2ffc8c3c992317d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8417"/><div sID="gen13540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8417"/><hi type="bold">30. sorrow, and the light is darkened--</hi>Otherwise, distress and light (that is, hope and fear) alternately succeed (as usually occurs in an unsettled state of things), and darkness arises in, &c. [Maurer].<div eID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavens--</hi>literally, "clouds," that is, its sky is rather "clouds" than sky. Otherwise from a different Hebrew root, "in its destruction" or ruins. Horsley takes "sea ... look unto the land" as a new image taken from mariners in a coasting vessel (such as all ancient vessels were), looking for the nearest land, which the darkness of the storm conceals, so that darkness and distress alone may be said to be visible. <chapter eID="Isa.5"/>

entries.8f253d66a491c8671cc20a030fdf56b96886d908: <div eID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26691" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26691" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with representing, in a beautiful parable, the tender care of God for his people, and their unworthy returns for his goodness, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7">Isa 5:1-7</reference>. The parable or allegory is then dropped; and the prophet, in plain terms, reproves and threatens them for their wickedness; particularly for their covetousness, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8-Isa.5.10">Isa 5:8-10</reference>; intemperance, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference>; and inattention to the warnings of Providence, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>. Then follows an enumeration of judgments as the necessary consequence. Captivity and famine appear with all their horrors, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Isa 5:13</reference>. Hades, or the grave, like a ravenous monster, opens wide its jaws, and swallows down its myriads, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>. Distress lays hold on all ranks, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.15">Isa 5:15</reference>; and God is glorified in the execution of his judgments, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.16">Isa 5:16</reference>; till the whole place is left desolate, a place for the flocks to range in, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Isa 5:17</reference>. The prophet then pauses; and again resumes his subject, reproving them for several other sins, and threatening them with woes and vengeance, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.18-Isa.5.24">Isa 5:18-24</reference>; after which he sums up the whole of his awful denunciation in a very lofty and spirited epiphonema or conclusion. The God of armies, having hitherto corrected to no purpose, is represented with inimitable majesty, as only giving a hist, and a swarm of nations hasten to his standard, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25-Isa.5.27">Isa 5:25-27</reference>. Upon a guilty race, unpitied by heaven or by earth, they execute their commission; and leave the land desolate and dark, without one ray of comfort to cheer the horrid gloom, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.28-Isa.5.30">Isa 5:28-30</reference>. <div eID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> This chapter likewise stands single and alone, unconnected with the preceding or following. The subject of it is nearly the same with that of the first chapter. It is a general reproof of the Jews for their wickedness; but it exceeds that chapter in force, in severity, in variety, and elegance; and it adds a more express declaration of vengeance by the Babylonian invasion. <div eID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> Now will I sing to my well-beloved a song of my beloved "Let me sing now a song," etc. - A MS., respectable for its antiquity, adds the word שיר shir, a song, after נא na; which gives so elegant a turn to the sentence by the repetition of it in the next member, and by distinguishing the members so exactly in the style and manner in the Hebrew poetical composition, that I am much inclined to think it genuine. <div eID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> A song of my beloved "A song of loves" - דודי dodey, for דודים dodim: status constructus pro absoluto, as the grammarians say, as <reference osisRef="Mic.6.16">Mic 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.66">Lam 3:66</reference>, so Archbishop Secker. Or rather, in all these and the like cases, a mistake of the transcribers, by not observing a small stroke, which in many MSS., is made to supply the מ mem, of the plural, thus, דודי dodi. שירת דודים shirath dodim is the same with שיר ידידת shir yedidoth, <reference osisRef="Psa.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>. In this way of understanding it we avoid the great impropriety of making the author of the song, and the person to whom it is addressed, to be the same. <div eID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> In a very fruitful hill "On a high and fruitful hill" - Hebrew בקרן בן שמן bekeren ben shamen, "on a horn the son of oil." The expression is highly descriptive and poetical. "He calls the land of Israel a horn, because it is higher than all lands; as the horn is higher than the whole body; and the son of oil, because it is said to be a land flowing with milk and honey." - Kimchi on the place. The parts of animals are, by an easy metaphor, applied to parts of the earth, both in common and poetical language. A promontory is called a cape or head; the Turks call it a nose. "Dorsum immane mari summo;" Virgil, a back, or ridge of rocks: - "Hanc latus angustum jam se cogentis in arctum <div eID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> Hesperiae tenuem producit in aequora linguam, <div eID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> Adriacas flexis claudit quae cornibus undas." <div eID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> Lucan, 2:612, of Brundusium, i.e., Βρεντεσιον, which, in the ancient language of that country, signifies stag's head, says Strabo. A horn is a proper and obvious image for a mountain or mountainous country. Solinus, cap. viii., says, "Italiam, ubi longius processerit, in cornua duo scindi;" that is, the high ridge of the Alps, which runs through the whole length of it, divides at last into two ridges, one going through Calabria, the other through the country of the Brutii. "Cornwall is called by the inhabitants in the British tongue Kernaw, as lessening by degrees like a horn, running out into promontories like so many horns. For the Britons call a horn corn, in the plural kern." - Camden. "And Sammes is of opinion, that the country had this name originally from the Phoenicians, who traded hither for tin; keren, in their language, being a horn." - Gibson. <div eID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> Here the precise idea seems to be that of a high mountain standing by itself; "vertex montis, aut pars montis ad aliis divisa;" which signification, says I. H. Michaelis, Bibl. Hallens., Not. in loc., the word has in Arabic. <div eID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26703" type="x-p"/> Judea was in general a mountainous country, whence Moses sometimes calls it The Mountain, "Thou shalt plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance;" <reference osisRef="Exo.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>. "I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land beyond Jordan; that goodly mountain, and Lebanon;" <reference osisRef="Deu.3.25">Deu 3:25</reference>. And in a political and religious view it was detached and separated from all the nations round it. Whoever has considered the descriptions given of Mount Tabor, (see Reland, Palaestin.; Eugene Roger, Terre Sainte, p. 64), and the views of it which are to be seen in books of travels, (Maundrell, p. 114; Egmont and Heyman, vol. ii., p. 25; Thevenot, vol. i., p. 429), its regular conic form rising singly in a plain to a great height, from a base small in proportion, and its beauty and fertility to the very top, will have a good idea of "a horn the son of oil;" and will perhaps be induced to think that the prophet took his image from that mountain.
entries.b70d80fee07aa0b009dc4c36a6c637a089f101aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26704" type="x-p"/> And gathered out the stones "And he cleared it from the stones" - This was agreeable to the husbandry: "Saxa, summa parte terrae, et vites et arbores laeduct; ima parte refrigerant;" Columell. de arb. 3: "Saxosum facile est expedire lectione lapidum;" Id. 2:2. "Lapides, qui supersunt, [al. insuper sunt], hieme rigent, aestate fervescunt; idcirco satis, arbustis, et vitibus nocent;" Pallad. 1:6. A piece of ground thus cleared of the stones Persius, in his hard way of metaphor, calls "exossatus ager," an unboned field; Sat. 6:52. <div eID="gen26704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26705" type="x-p"/> The choicest vine "Sorek" - Many of the ancient interpreters, the Septuagint, Aquila, and Theod., have retained this word as a proper name; I think very rightly. Sorek was a valley lying between Ascalon and Gaza, and running far up eastward in the tribe of Judah. Both Ascalon and Gaza were anciently famous for wine; the former is mentioned as such by Alexander Trallianus; the latter by several authors, quoted by Reland, Palaest., p. 589 and 986. And it seems that the upper part of the valley of Sorek, and that of Eshcol, where the spies gathered the single cluster of grapes, which they were obliged to bear between two upon a staff, being both near to Hebron were in the same neighborhood, and that all this part of the country abounded with rich vineyards. Compare <reference osisRef="Num.13.22">Num 13:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.23">Num 13:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.3">Jdg 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.4">Jdg 16:4</reference>. P. Nau supposes Eshcol and Sorek to be only different names for the same valley. Voyage Noveau de la Terre Sainte, lib. iv., chap. 18. See likewise De Lisle's posthumous map of the Holy Land. Paris, 1763. See Bochart, Hieroz. ii., Colossians 725. Thevenot, i, p. 406. Michaelis (note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.4">Jdg 16:4</reference> (note), German translation) thinks it probable, from some circumstances of the history there given, that Sorek was in the tribe of Judah, not in the country of the Philistines. <div eID="gen26705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26706" type="x-p"/> The vine of Sorek was known to the Israelites, being mentioned by Moses, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen 49:11</reference>, before their coming out of Egypt. Egypt was not a wine country. "Throughout this country there are no wines;" Sandys, p. 101. At least in very ancient times they had none. Herodotus, 2:77, says it had no vines and therefore used an artificial wine made of barley. That is not strictly true, for the vines of Egypt are spoken of in Scripture, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.47">Psa 78:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.105.33">Psa 105:33</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Gen.40.11">Gen 40:11</reference>, by which it should seem that they drank only the fresh juice pressed from the grape, which was called οινος αμπελινος; Herodot., 2:37. But they had no large vineyards, nor was the country proper for them, being little more than one large plain, annually overflowed by the Nile. The Mareotic in later times is, I think, the only celebrated Egyptian wine which we meet with in history. The vine was formerly, as Hasselquist tells us it is now, "cultivated in Egypt for the sake of eating the grapes, not for wine, which is brought from Candia," etc. "They were supplied with wine from Greece, and likewise from Phoenicia," Herodot., 3:6. The vine and the wine of Sorek therefore, which lay near at hand for importation into Egypt, must in all probability have been well known to the Israelites, when they sojourned there. There is something remarkable in the manner in which Moses, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen 49:11</reference>, makes mention of it, which, for want of considering this matter, has not been attended to; it is in Jacob's prophecy of the future prosperity of the tribe of Judah: - "Binding his foal to the vine, <div eID="gen26706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26707" type="x-p"/> And his ass's colt to his own sorek; <div eID="gen26707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26708" type="x-p"/> He washeth his raiment in wine, <div eID="gen26708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26709" type="x-p"/> And his cloak in the blood of grapes." <div eID="gen26709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26710" type="x-p"/> I take the liberty of rendering שרקה sorekah, for שרקו soreko, his sorek, as the Masoretes do by pointing עירה iroh, for עירו iro, his foal. עיר ir, might naturally enough appear in the feminine form; but it is not at all probable that שרק sorek ever should. By naming particularly the vine of Sorek, and as the vine belonging to Judah, the prophecy intimates the very part of the country which was to fall to the lot of that tribe. Sir John Chardin says, "that at Casbin, a city of Persia, they turn their cattle into the vineyards after the vintage, to browse on the vines." He speaks also of vines in that country so large that he could hardly compass the trunks of them with his arms. Voyages, tom. iii., p. 12, 12mo. This shows that the ass might be securely bound to the vine, and without danger of damaging the tree by browsing on it. <div eID="gen26710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26711" type="x-p"/> And built a tower in the midst of it - Our Savior, who has taken the general idea of one of his parables, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.33">Mat 21:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.12.1">Mar 12:1</reference>, from this of Isaiah, has likewise inserted this circumstance of building a tower; which is generally explained by commentators as designed for the keeper of the vineyard to watch and defend the fruits. But for this purpose it was usual to make a little temporary hut, (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>), which might serve for the short season while the fruit was ripening, and which was removed afterwards. The tower therefore should rather mean a building of a more permanent nature and use; the farm, as we may call it, of the vineyard, containing all the offices and implements, and the whole apparatus necessary for the culture of the vineyard, and the making of the wine. To which image in the allegory, the situation the manner of building, the use, and the whole service of the temple, exactly answered. And so the Chaldee paraphrast very rightly expounds it: Et statui eos (Israelitas) ut plantam vineae selectae et aedificavi Sanctuarium meum in medio illorum. "And I have appointed the Israelites as a plant of a chosen vine, and I have built my sanctuary in the midst of them." So also Hieron. in loc. Aedificavit quoque turrim in medio ejus; templum videlicet in media civitate. "He built also a tower in the midst of it, viz., his own temple in the midst of the city." That they have still such towers or buildings for use or pleasure, in their gardens in the East, see Harmer's Observations, 2 p. 241. <div eID="gen26711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26712" type="x-p"/> And also made a wine-press therein. "And hewed out a lake therein" - This image also our Savior has preserved in his parable. יקב yekeb; the Septuagint render it here προληνιον, and in four other places ὑποληνιον, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">Isa 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joe.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.17">Hag 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zac.14.10">Zac 14:10</reference>, I think more properly; and this latter word St. Mark uses. It means not the wine-press itself, or calcatorium, which is called גת gath, or פורה purah; but what the Romans called lacus, the lake; the large open place or vessel, which by a conduit or spout received the must from the wine-press. In very hot countries it was perhaps necessary, or at least very convenient, to have the lake under ground, or in a cave hewed out of the side of the rock, for coolness, that the heat might not cause too great a fermentation, and sour the must. Vini confectio instituitur in cella, vel intimae domus camera quadam a ventorum ingressu remota. Kempfer, of Shiras wine. Amaen. Exot. p. 376. For the wind, to which that country is subject, would injure the wine. "The wine-presses in Persia," says Sir John Chardin, "are formed by making hollow places in the ground, lined with masons' work." Harmer's Observations, i., p. 392. See a print of one in Kempfer, p. 377. <div eID="gen26712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26713" type="x-p"/> Nonnus describes at large Bacchus hollowing the inside of a rock, and hewing out a place for the wine-press, or rather the lake: - Και σκοπελους ελαχηνε· πεδοσκαφεος δε σιδηρου Θηγαλεῃ γλωχινι μυχον κοιληνατο πετρης· Λειηνας δε μετωπα βαθυνομενων κενεωνων Αφρον [f. ακρον] εΰστραφυλοιο τυπον ποιησατο λενου. <div eID="gen26713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26714" type="x-p"/> Dionysiac. lib. xii., 50:331. "He pierced the rock; and with the sharpen'd tool <div eID="gen26714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26715" type="x-p"/> Of steel well-temper'd scoop'd its inmost depth: <div eID="gen26715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26716" type="x-p"/> Then smooth'd the front, and form'd the dark recess <div eID="gen26716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26717" type="x-p"/> In just dimensions for the foaming lake." <div eID="gen26717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26718" type="x-p"/> And he looked "And he expected" - Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer 2:21</reference>, uses the same image, and applies it to the same purpose, in an elegant paraphrase of this part of Isaiah's parable, in his flowing and plaintive manner: - "But I planted thee a sorek, a scion perfectly genuine: How then art thou changed, and become to me the degenerate shoots of the strange vine!" <div eID="gen26718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26719" type="x-p"/> Wild grapes "poisonous berries" - באשים beushim, not merely useless, unprofitable grapes, such as wild grapes; but grapes offensive to the smell, noxious, poisonous. By the force and intent of the allegory, to good grapes ought to be opposed fruit of a dangerous and pernicious quality; as, in the explication of it, to judgment is opposed tyranny, and to righteousness, oppression. גפן gephen, the vine, is a common name or genus, including several species under it; and Moses, to distinguish the true vine, or that from which wine is made, from the rest. calls it, <reference osisRef="Num.6.4">Num 6:4</reference>, גפן היין gephen haiyayin, the wine-vine. Some of the other sorts were of a poisonous quality, as appears from the story related among the miraculous acts of Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.39-2Kgs.4.41">2Kgs 4:39-41</reference>. "And one went out into the field to gather potherbs; and he found a Seld vine, and he gathered from it wild fruit, his lapful; and he went and shred them into the pot of pottage, for they knew them not. And they poured it out for the men to eat: and it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out and said, There is death in the pot, O man of God; and they could not eat of it. And he said, Bring meal, (leg. קחו kechu, nine MSS., one edition), and he threw it into the pot. And he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was nothing hurtful in the pot." <div eID="gen26719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26720" type="x-p"/> From some such sorts of poisonous fruits of the grape kind Moses has taken these strong and highly poetical images, with which he has set forth the future corruption and extreme degeneracy of the Israelites, in an allegory which has a near relation, both in its subject and imagery, to this of Isaiah: <reference osisRef="Deu.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.33">Deu 32:33</reference>. "Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, <div eID="gen26720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26721" type="x-p"/> And from the fields of Gomorrah: <div eID="gen26721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26722" type="x-p"/> Their grapes are grapes of gall; <div eID="gen26722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26723" type="x-p"/> Their clusters are bitter: <div eID="gen26723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26724" type="x-p"/> Their wine is the poison of dragons, <div eID="gen26724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26725" type="x-p"/> And the cruel venom of aspics." "I am inclined to believe," says Hasselquist, "that the prophet here, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2-Isa.5.4">Isa 5:2-4</reference>, means the hoary nightshade, solanum incanum; because it is common in Egypt, Palestine, and the East; and the Arabian name agrees well with it. The Arabs call it anab el dib, i.e., wolf grapes. The באושים beushim, says Rab. Chai., is a well known species of the vine, and the worst of all sorts. The prophet could not have found a plant more opposite to the vine than this; for it grows much in the vineyards, and is very pernicious to them; wherefore they root it out: it likewise resembles a vine by its shrubby stalk;" Travels, p. 289. See also Michaelis Questions aux Voyageurs Danois, No. 64.
entries.cba5ee711e32a0bed508f7a068bae0a82379087c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26726" type="x-p"/> Inhabitants - ישבי yoshebey, in the plural number; three MSS., (two ancient), and so likewise the Septuagint and Vulgate.
entries.7de23bb324c5625ef0eb68254ac8f2e8009fce45: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26727" type="x-p"/> There shall come up briers and thorns "The thorn shall spring up in it" - One MS. has בשמיר beshamir. The true reading seems to be בו שמור bo shamir, which is confirmed by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate.
entries.97dbedd7341aaa6c3eac26e74fc1bd5a41657c19: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26728" type="x-p"/> And he looked for judgment - The paronomasia, or play on the words, in this place, is very remarkable; mishpat, mishpach, tsedakah, tseakah. There are many examples of it in the other prophets, but Isaiah seems peculiarly fond of it. See <reference osisRef="Isa.13.6">Isa 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17">Isa 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.7">Isa 32:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.6">Isa 57:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Isa 65:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.12">Isa 65:12</reference>. Rabbi David Kimchi has noticed the paronomasia here: he expected משפט mishpat, judgment, but behold משפח mishpach, oppression; he expected צדקה tsedakah, righteousness, but behold צעקה tseakah, a cry. The rabbins esteem it a great beauty; their term for it is צחות הלשון tsachoth haltashon, elegance of language. <div eID="gen26728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26729" type="x-p"/> Oppression "tyranny" - משפח mishpach, from שפח shaphach, servum fecit, Arab. Houbigant: שפחה shiphchah is serva, a handmaid or female slave. משפח mispach, eighteen MSS.
entries.33f62943d5730c1f55bbb27853cd95948dc89be6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26730" type="x-p"/> Wo unto them that - lay field to field "You who lay field unto field" - Read תקריבו takribu, in the second person; to answer to the verb following. So Vulgate.
entries.b7946d11bb0b3abc06bbf790b172dc4b59add6b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26731" type="x-p"/> In mine ears. "To mine ear" - The sentence in the Hebrew text seems to be imperfect in this place; as likewise in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Isa 22:14</reference> (note), where the very same sense seems to be required as here. See the note there; and compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sam 9:15</reference> (note). In this place the Septuagint supply the word ηκουσθη, and the Syriac אשתמע eshtama, auditus est Jehovah in auribus meis, i.e., נגלה niglah, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Isa 22:14</reference>. <div eID="gen26731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26732" type="x-p"/> Many houses - This has reference to what was said in the preceding verse: "In vain are ye so intent upon joining house to house, and field to field; your houses shall be left uninhabited, and your fields shall become desolate and barren; so that a vineyard of ten acres shall produce but one bath (not eight gallons) of wine, and the husbandman shall reap but a tenth part of the seed which he has sown." Kimchi says this means such an extent of vineyard as would require ten yoke of oxen to plough in one day.
entries.f2e04c4845545aeb493155b50093bb4c712fe389: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26733" type="x-p"/> Wo unto them that rise up early - There is a likeness between this and the following passage of the prophet Amos, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.3-Amo.6.6">Amo 6:3-6</reference>, who probably wrote before Isaiah. If the latter be the copier, he seems hardly to have equalled the elegance of the original: - "Ye that put far away the evil day <div eID="gen26733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26734" type="x-p"/> And affect the seat of violence; <div eID="gen26734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26735" type="x-p"/> Who lie upon beds of ivory, <div eID="gen26735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26736" type="x-p"/> And stretch yourselves upon your couches; <div eID="gen26736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26737" type="x-p"/> And eat the lambs from the flock, <div eID="gen26737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26738" type="x-p"/> And calves from the midst of the stall; <div eID="gen26738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26739" type="x-p"/> Who chant to the sound of the viol, <div eID="gen26739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26740" type="x-p"/> And like David invent for yourselves instruments of music; <div eID="gen26740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26741" type="x-p"/> Who quaff wine in large bowls, <div eID="gen26741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26742" type="x-p"/> And are anointed with the choicest ointments: <div eID="gen26742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26743" type="x-p"/> But are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph." <div eID="gen26743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26744" type="x-p"/> Kimchi says, "they consider not the heavens nor their hosts: they pray not the morning nor the evening prayer unto the Lord." <div eID="gen26744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26745" type="x-p"/> Follow strong drink - Theodoret and Chrysostom on this place, both Syrians, and unexceptionable witnesses in what belongs to their own country, inform us that שכר shechar (σικερα in the Greek of both Testaments, rendered by us by the general term strong drink) meant properly palm wine, or date wine, which was and is still much in use in the Eastern countries. Judea was famous for the abundance and excellence of its palm trees; and consequently had plenty of this wine. "Fiunt (vina) et e pomis; primumque e palmis, quo Parthi et Indi utun tur, et oriens totus: maturarum modio in aquae congiis tribus macerato expressoque." Plin. lib. 14:19. "Ab his cariotae [palmae] maxime celebrantur; et cibo quidem, sed et succo, uberrimae. Ex quibus praecipua vina orienti; iniqua capiti, unde porno nomen." Id. 13:9. Καρος signifies stupefaction: and in Hebrew likewise the wine has its name from its remarkably inebriating quality.
entries.f1a8732a1544cc9c00a7e741fb58e9ddbc16b0c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26746" type="x-p"/> And their honorable men "And the nobles" - These verses have likewise a reference to the two preceding. They that indulged in feasting and drinking shall perish with hunger and thirst; and Hades shall indulge his appetite as much as they had done, and devour them all. The image is strong and expressive in the highest degree. <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>, uses the same image with great force: - the ambitious and avaricious conqueror. "Enlargeth his appetite like Hades; <div eID="gen26746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26747" type="x-p"/> And he is like Death, and will never be satisfied," <div eID="gen26747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26748" type="x-p"/> But, in Isaiah, Hades is introduced to much greater advantage, in person; and placed before our eyes in the form of a ravenous monster, opening wide his immeasurable jaws, and swallowing them all together: "Therefore Shoel hath dilated her soul, she hath opened her mouth beyond limit." Destruction expects more than a common meal, when God visits Jerusalem for her iniquities. This seems to refer to the ruin brought on the Jews by the Romans. Our blessed Lord repeats this parable, and applies it to this very transaction, <reference osisRef="Mat.21.33">Mat 21:33</reference>.
entries.eb17ce3b38462f9181621dec06c4c33f420a482f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen26748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26749" type="x-p"/> The lambs "And the kids" - גרים gerim, "strangers." The Septuagint read, more agreeably to the design of the prophet, כרים carim, αρνες, "the lambs." גדים gedayim, "the kids," Dr. Durell; nearer to the present reading: and so Archbishop Secker. The meaning is, their luxurious habitations shall be so entirely destroyed as to become a pasture for flocks. <div eID="gen26749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26750" type="x-p"/> After their manner "Without restraint" - כדברם kedobram, secundum duetum eorum; i.e. suo ipsorum ductu; as their own will shall lead them.
entries.d77bf4d4140950f244a218633e3e609a4524ebf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen26750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26751" type="x-p"/> With a cart-rope "As a long cable" - The Septuagint, Aquila, Sym., and Theod., for בחבלי bechabley, read כחבלי kechahley, ὡς σχοινιῳ, or σχοινιοις; and the Septuagint, instead of שוא shau, read some other word signifying long; ὡς σχοινιῳ μακρῳ; and so likewise the Syriac, אריכא arecha. Houbigant conjectures that the word which the Septuagint had in their copies was שרוע sarua, which is used <reference osisRef="Lev.21.18">Lev 21:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.23">Lev 22:23</reference>, for something in an animal body superfluous, lengthened beyond its natural measure. And he explains it of sin added to sin, and one sin drawing on another, till the whole comes to an enormous length and magnitude; compared to the work of a rope-maker still increasing and lengthening his rope, with the continued addition of new materials. "Eos propheta similes facit homini restiario, qui funem torquet, cannabe addita et contorta, eadem iterans, donec funem in longum duxerit, neque eum liceat protrahi longius." "An evil inclination," says Kimchi on this place, from the ancient rabbins, "is at the beginning like a fine hair-string, but at the finishing like a thick cart-rope." By a long progression in iniquity, and a continued accumulation of sin, men arrive at length to the highest degree of wickedness; bidding open defiance to God, and scoffing at his threatened judgments, as it is finely expressed in the next verse. The Chaldee paraphrast explains it in the same manner, of wickedness increasing from small beginnings, till it arrives to a great magnitude. - L. <div eID="gen26751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26752" type="x-p"/> I believe neither the rabbins nor Bishop Lowth have hit on the true meaning of this place, the prophet seems to refer to idol sacrifices. The victims they offered were splendidly decked out for the sacrifice. Their horns and hoofs were often gilded, and their heads dressed out with fillets and garlands. The cords of vanity may refer to the silken strings by which they were led to the altar, some of which were unusually thick. The offering for iniquity was adorned with fillets and garlands; the sin-offering with silken cords, like unto cart-ropes. Pride, in their acts of humiliation, had the upper hand.
entries.b3754cef1c59de3cc4e39c4448f6d64cb8833fb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen26752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26753" type="x-p"/> Let the counsel of the Holy One - Tryphiodorus has an expression something like this: - - επει Διος ηλυθε βουλη. <div eID="gen26753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26754" type="x-p"/> Tryph. Il Excid. 239. <div eID="gen26754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26755" type="x-p"/> Because the counsel of Jupiter was come. "This expression, ηλυθε βουλη, is, I believe, something uncommon; but it is exactly paralleled and explained by a passage in Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>. The Septuagint has expressed it in the very same words with Tryphiodorus: και ελθοι ἡ βουλ η του ἁγιου Ισραηλ, ἱνα γνωμεν." - Merrick's note, ad loc.
entries.7bd333b84678258943ac6aa739759b6ffff316cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen26755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26756" type="x-p"/> Mighty to drink wine - "They show not," says Kimchi, "their strength in combating their enemies, but in drunkenness and debauchery."
entries.db2d51b54b25d129bf028d0d6924e492d5bbb72e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen26756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26757" type="x-p"/> The righteous - צדיק tsaddik, singular, Sept. Vulg., and two editions.
entries.cc7f51c57bf580aefaafdaa763bfc2ca3c0b3349: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen26757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26758" type="x-p"/> The flame "The tongue of fire" - "The flame, because it is in the shape of a tongue; and so it is called metaphorically." Sal. ben Melec. The metaphor is so exceedingly obvious, as well as beautiful, that one may wonder that it has not been more frequently used. Virgil very elegantly intimates, rather than expresses, the image; - <div eID="gen26758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26759" type="x-p"/> Ecce levis summo de vertice visus Iuli <div eID="gen26759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26760" type="x-p"/> Fundere lumen apex; tactuque innoxia molli <div eID="gen26760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26761" type="x-p"/> Lambere flamma comas, et circum tempora pasci. <div eID="gen26761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26762" type="x-p"/> Aen. 2:682. "Strange to relate! from young Iulus' head <div eID="gen26762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26763" type="x-p"/> A lambent flame arose, which gently spread <div eID="gen26763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26764" type="x-p"/> Around his brows, and on his temples fed." <div eID="gen26764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> And more boldly of Aetna darting out flames from its top: - <div eID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26766" type="x-p"/> Interdumque atram prorumpit ad aethera nubem, <div eID="gen26766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26767" type="x-p"/> Turbine fumantem piceo, et candente favilla: <div eID="gen26767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26768" type="x-p"/> Attollitque globos flammarum, et sidera lambit. <div eID="gen26768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26769" type="x-p"/> Aen. 3:574. "By turns a pitchy cloud she rolls on high, <div eID="gen26769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26770" type="x-p"/> By turns hot embers from her entrails fly, <div eID="gen26770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26771" type="x-p"/> And flakes of mountain flames, that lick the sky." <div eID="gen26771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26772" type="x-p"/> The disparted tongues, as it were of fire, <reference osisRef="Act.2.3">Act 2:3</reference>, which appeared at the descent of the Holy Spirit, on the apostles, give the same idea; that is, of flames shooting diversely into pyramidal forms, or points, like tongues. It may be farther observed that the prophet in this place has given the metaphor its full force, in applying it to the action of fire in eating up and devouring whatever comes in its way, like a ravenous animal whose tongue is principally employed in taking in his food or prey; which image Moses has strongly exhibited in an expressive comparison: "And Moab said to the elders of Midian Now shall this collection of people lick up all that are around about us, as the ox licketh up the grass of the field," <reference osisRef="Num.22.4">Num 22:4</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.38">1Kgs 18:38</reference>. <div eID="gen26772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26773" type="x-p"/> Their root shall be as rottenness - כמק cammak, like mak; whence probably our word muck, dung, was derived.
entries.17fad6f21988f2b46f8d77332e2049ceb8d41627: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen26773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26774" type="x-p"/> The hills did tremble "And the mountains trembled" - Probably referring to the great earthquakes in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, in or not long before the time of the prophet himself, recorded as a remarkable era in the title of the prophecies of Amos., <reference osisRef="Amo.1.1">Amo 1:1</reference>, and by Zechariah, <reference osisRef="Zac.14.5">Zac 14:5</reference>.
entries.471057358fbd62bd66acc8bd58aaf3652f202eae: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen26774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26775" type="x-p"/> He will - hiss "He will hist" - "The metaphor is taken from the practice of those that keep bees, who draw them out of their hives into the fields, and lead them back again, συρισμασι, by a hiss or a whistle." - Cyril, on this place; and to the same purpose Theodoret, ib. In <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>, the metaphor is more apparent, by being carried farther, where the hostile armies are expressed by the fly and the bee: - "Jehovah shall hist the fly That is in the utmost parts of Egypt; And the bee, that is in the land of Assyria." <div eID="gen26775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26776" type="x-p"/> On which place see <reference osisRef="Deu.1.44">Deu 1:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>; and God calls the locusts his great army, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.25">Joe 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.23.28">Exo 23:28</reference>. See Huet, Quest. Alnet. 2:12. שרק sharak or shrak, he shall whistle for them, call loud and shrill; he shall shriek, and they (their enemies) shall come at his call. <div eID="gen26776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> With speed - This refers to the <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>. As the scoffers had challenged God to make speed, and to hasten his work of vengeance, so now God assures them that with speed and swiftly it shall come.
entries.03207c58b8afdbfe16d3d63d386c7c19ef5ca64d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26778" type="x-p"/> None - among them - Kimchi has well illustrated this continued exaggeration or hyperbole, as he rightly calls it, to the following effect: "Through the greatness of their courage they shall not be fatigued with their march, nor shall they stumble though they march with the utmost speed: they shall not slumber by day, nor sleep by night; neither shall they ungird their armor, or put off their sandals to take their rest. Their arms shall be always in readiness, their arrows sharpened, and their bows bent. The hoofs of their horses are hard as a rock. They shall not fail, or need to be shod with iron: the wheels of their carriages shall move as rapidly as a whirlwind." <div eID="gen26778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26779" type="x-p"/> Neither shall the girdle - The Eastern people, wearing long and loose garments, were unfit for action or business of any kind, without girding their clothes about them. When their business was finished they took off their girdles. A girdle therefore denotes strength and activity; and to unloose the girdle is to deprive of strength, to render unfit for action. God promises to unloose the loins of kings before Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">Isa 45:1</reference>. The girdle is so essential a part of a soldier's accoutrements, being the last that he puts on to make himself ready for action, that to be girded, ζωννυσθαι, with the Greeks means to be completely armed and ready for battle: - Ατρειδης δ εβοησεν, ιδε ζωννυσθαι ανωγεν Αργειους. <div eID="gen26779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26780" type="x-p"/> Iliad, 11:15. Το δε ενδυναι τα ὁπλα εκαλουν οἱ παλαιοι ζωννυσθαι. <div eID="gen26780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26781" type="x-p"/> Pausan. Boeot. <div eID="gen26781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26782" type="x-p"/> It is used in the same manner by the Hebrews: "Let not him that girdeth himself boast as he that unlooseth his girdle," <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.11">1Kgs 20:11</reference>; that is, triumph not before the war is finished.
entries.379c3b90be3f319ab7edd4d8bf1b1f6d2f412977: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen26782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26783" type="x-p"/> Their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint "The hoofs of their horses shall be counted as adamant" - The shoeing of horses with iron plates nailed to the hoof is quite a modern practice, and was unknown to the ancients, as appears from the silence of the Greek and Roman writers, especially those that treat of horse medicine, who could not have passed over a matter so obvious and of such importance that now the whole science takes its name from it, being called by us farriery. The horseshoes of leather and iron which are mentioned; the silver and gold shoes with which Nero and Poppaea shod their mules, used occasionally to preserve the hoofs of delicate cattle, or for vanity, were of a very different kind; they enclosed the whole hoof as in a case, or as a shoe does a man's foot, and were bound or tied on. For this reason the strength, firmness and solidity of a horse's hoof was of much greater importance with them than with us, and was esteemed one of the first praises of a fine horse. Xenophon says that a good horse's hoof is hard, hollow, and sounds upon the ground like a cymbal. Hence the χαλκοποδες ἱπποι, of Homer, and Virgil's solido graviter sonat ungula cornu. And Xenophon gives directions for hardening the horses' hoofs by making the pavement on which he stands in the stable with roundheaded stones. For want of this artificial defense to the foot which our horses have, Amos, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.12">Amo 6:12</reference>, speaks of it as a thing as much impracticable to make horses run upon a hard rock as to plough up the same rock with oxen: - "Shall horses run upon a rock? <div eID="gen26783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26784" type="x-p"/> Shall one plough it up with oxen?" <div eID="gen26784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26785" type="x-p"/> These circumstances must be taken into consideration in order to give us a full notion of the propriety and force of the image by which the prophet sets forth the strength and excellence of the Babylonish cavalry, which made a great part of the strength of the Assyrian army. Xenop. Cyrop. lib. ii. <div eID="gen26785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26786" type="x-p"/> Like a whirlwind - כסופה cassuphah, like the stormy blast. Here sense and sound are well connected.
entries.edef064e8dac7b7cc5c6c22322f70eeb41c4b616: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen26786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26787" type="x-p"/> If one look unto the land, etc. "And these shall look to the heaven upward, and down to the earth" - ונבט לארץ venibbat laarets. Και εμβλεψονται εις την γην. So the Septuagint, according to the Vatican and Alexandrian copies; but the Complutensian and Aldine editions have it more fully, thus: - Και εμβλεψονται εις τον ουρανον ανω, και κατω; and the Arabic from the Septuagint, as if it had stood thus: Και εμβλεψονται εις ουρανον, και εις την γην κατω, both of which are plainly defective; the words εις την γην, unto the earth, being wanted in the former, and the word ανω, above, in the latter. But an ancient Coptic version from the Septuagint, supposed to be of the second century, some fragments of which are preserved in the library of St. Germain des Prez at Paris, completes the sentence; for, according to this version, it stood thus in the Septuagint. - Και εμβλεψονται εις τον ουρανον ανω, και εις την γην κατω; "And they shall look unto the heavens above and unto the earth beneath," and so it stands in the Septuagint MSS., Pachom. and 1. D. II., according to which they must have read their Hebrew text in this manner: - ונבט לשמים למעלה ולארץ למטה. This is probably the true reading, with which I have made the translation agree. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">Isa 8:22</reference>; where the same sense is expressed in regard to both particulars, which are here equally and highly proper, the looking upwards, as well as down to the earth: but the form of expression is varied. I believe the Hebrew text in that place to be right, though not so full as I suppose it was originally here; and that of the Septuagint there to be redundant, being as full as the Coptic version and MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2 represent it in this place, from which I suppose it has been interpolated. <div eID="gen26787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26788" type="x-p"/> Darkness "The gloomy vapor" - The Syriac and Vulgate seem to have read בערפלח bearphalach; but Jarchi explains the present reading as signifying darkness; and possibly the Syriac and Vulgate may have understood it in the same manner.  <chapter eID="Isa.5"/> <div eID="gen26788" type="x-p"/>

entries.82754595d39078e1e78288fa2d3b8f80107afe85: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.2">Isa 5:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen12849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12850" type="x-p"/> The prophet commenced his first address in chapter 1 like another Moses; the second, which covered no less ground, he opened with the text of an earlier prophecy; and now he commences the third like a musician, addressing both himself and his hearers with enticing words. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa 1:1</reference></hi>. <hi type="italic">“Arise, I will sing of my beloved, a song of my dearest touching his vineyard.”</hi> The fugitive rhythm, the musical euphony, the charming assonances in this appeal, it is impossible to reproduce. They are perfectly inimitable. The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">lı̄dı̄dı̄</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> <hi type="italic">objecti</hi>. The person to whom the song referred, to whom it applied, of whom it treated, was the singer’s own beloved. It was a song of his dearest one (not his cousin, <hi type="italic">patruelis</hi>, as Luther renders it in imitation of the Vulgate, for the meaning of <hi type="italic">dōd</hi> is determined by <hi type="italic">yâdid</hi>, beloved) touching his vineyard. The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">l'carmo</hi> is also <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> <hi type="italic">objecti</hi>. The song of the beloved is really a song concerning the vineyard of the beloved; and this song is a song of the beloved himself, not a song written about him, or attributed to him, but such a song as he himself had sung, and still had to sing. The prophet, by beginning in this manner, was surrounded (either in spirit or in outward reality) by a crowd of people from Jerusalem and Judah. The song is a short one, and runs thus in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa 1:1</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa 1:2</reference> : <hi type="italic">“My beloved had a vineyard on a fatly nourished mountain-horn, and dug it up and cleared it of stones, and planted it with noble vines, and built a tower in it, and also hewed out a wine-press therein; and hoped that it would bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.”</hi> The vineyard was situated upon a <hi type="italic">keren</hi>, i.e., upon a prominent mountain peak projecting like a horn, and therefore open to the sun on all sides; for, as Virgil says in the <hi type="italic">Georgics</hi>, “<hi type="italic">apertos Bacchus amat colles</hi>.” This mountain horn was <hi type="italic">ben</hi>-<hi type="italic">shemen</hi>, a child of fatness: the fatness was innate, it belonged to it by nature (<hi type="italic">shemen</hi> is used, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>, to denote the fertility of a nutritive loamy soil). And the owner of the vineyard spared no attention or trouble. The plough could not be used, from the steepness of the mountain slope: he therefore dug it up, that is to say, he turned up the soil which was to be made into a vineyard with a hoe (<hi type="italic">izzēk</hi>, to hoe; Arab. <hi type="italic">mi‛zak</hi>, <hi type="italic">mi‛zaka</hi>); and as he found it choked up with stones and boulders, he got rid of this rubbish by throwing it out <hi type="italic">sikkēl</hi>, a privative <hi type="italic">piel</hi>, <hi type="italic">lapidibus purgare</hi>, then <hi type="italic">operam consumere in lapides</hi>, sc. <hi type="italic">ejiciendos</hi>, to stone, or clear of stones: Ges. §52, 2). After the soil had been prepared he planted it with <hi type="italic">sorek</hi>, i.e., the finest kind of eastern vine, bearing small grapes of a bluish-red, with pips hardly perceptible to the tongue. The name is derived from its colour (compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">zerka</hi>, red wine). To protect and adorn the vineyard which had been so richly planted, he built a tower in the midst of it. The expression <hi type="italic">“and also”</hi> calls especial attention to the fact that he hewed out a wine-trough therein (<hi type="italic">yekeb</hi>, the trough into which the must or juice pressed from the grapes in the wine-press flows, <hi type="italic">lacus</hi> as distinguished from <hi type="italic">torcular</hi>); that is to say, in order that the trough might be all the more fixed and durable, he constructed it in a rocky portion of the ground (<hi type="italic">Châtsēb</hi> <hi type="italic">bo</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Chătsab</hi> <hi type="italic">bo</hi>, with <hi type="italic">a</hi> and the accent drawn back, because a <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> was thereby easily rendered inaudible, so that <hi type="italic">Châtsēb</hi> is not a participial adjective, as Böttcher supposes). This was a difficult task, as the expression “and also” indicates; and for that very reason it was an evidence of the most confident expectation. But how bitterly was this deceived! The vineyard produced no such fruit, as might have been expected from a <hi type="italic">sorek</hi> plantation; it brought forth no <hi type="italic">‛anâbim</hi> whatever, i.e., no such grapes as a cultivated vine should bear, but only <hi type="italic">b'ushim</hi>, or wild grapes. Luther first of all adopted the rendering <hi type="italic">wild grapes</hi>, and then altered it to harsh or sour grapes. But it comes to the same thing. The difference between a wild vine and a good vine is only qualitative. The <hi type="italic">vitis vinifera</hi>, like all cultivated plants, is assigned to the care of man, under which it improves; whereas in its wild state it remains behind its true intention (see <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, §622). Consequently the word <hi type="italic">b'ushim</hi> (from <hi type="italic">bâ'ash</hi>, to be bad, or smell bad) denotes not only the grapes of the wild vine, which are naturally small and harsh (Rashi, <hi type="italic">lambruches</hi>, i.e., grapes of the <hi type="italic">labrusca</hi>, which is used now, however, as the botanical name of a vine that is American in its origin), but also grapes of a good stock, which have either been spoiled or have failed to ripen.<note placement="foot">In the Jerusalem <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> such grapes are called <hi type="italic">ūbshin</hi>, the letters being transposed; and in the Mishnah (<hi type="italic">Ma'aseroth</hi> i. 2, <hi type="italic">Zebî'ith</hi> iv 8) הבאישׁ is the standing word applied to grapes that are only half ripe (see Löwy’s <hi type="italic">Leshon Chachamim</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Wörterbuch des talmudischen Hebräisch</hi>, Prag 1845). With reference to the wild grape (τὸ ἀγριόκλημα), a writer, describing the useful plants of Greece, says, “Its fruit (τὰ ἀγριοστάφυλα) consists of very small berries, not much larger than bilberries, with a harsh flavour.”</note> <div eID="gen12850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12851" type="x-p"/> These were the grapes which the vineyard produced, such as you might indeed have expected from a wild vine, but not from carefully cultivated vines of the very choicest kind.
entries.d4495cfabebd48f1038aa4e3628f56cbbb441877: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3-Isa.5.4">Isa 5:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen12851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12852" type="x-p"/> The song of the beloved who was so sorely deceived terminates here. The prophet recited it, not his beloved himself; but as they were both of one heart and one soul, the prophet proceeds thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">Isa 5:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, between me and my vineyard! What could have been done more to my vineyard that I have not done in it? Wherefore did I hope that it would bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes?”</hi> The fact that the prophet speaks as if he were the beloved himself, shows at once who the beloved must be. The beloved of the prophet and the lover of the prophet (<hi type="italic">yâdid</hi> and <hi type="italic">dōd</hi>) were Jehovah, with whom he was so united by a <hi type="italic">union mystica</hi> exalted above all earthly love, that, like the angel of Jehovah in the early histories, he could speak as if he were Jehovah Himself (see especially Zec 2:12-13). To any one with spiritual intuition, therefore, the parabolical meaning and object of the song would be at once apparent; and even the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the men of Judah (yoosheeb and iish are used collectively, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Isa 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">Isa 22:21</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.20.6">Isa 20:6</reference>) were not so stupefied by sin, that they could not perceive to what the prophet was leading. It was for them to decide where the guilt of this unnatural issue lay - that is to say, of this thorough contradiction between the “doing” of the vineyard and the “doing” of the Lord; that instead of the grapes he hoped for, it brought forth wild grapes. (On the expression “what could have been done,” <hi type="italic">quid faciendum est</hi>, <hi type="italic">mah</hi>-<hi type="italic">la'asoth</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Hab.1.17">Hab 1:17</reference>, Ges. §132, Anm. 1.) Instead of למה (למּה) we have the more suitable term מדּוּע, the latter being used in relation to the actual cause (<hi type="italic">Causa efficiens</hi>), the former in relation to the object (<hi type="italic">Causa finalis</hi>). The parallel to the second part, viz., <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference>, resembles the passage before us, not only in the use of this particular word, but also in the fact that there, as well as here, it relates to both clauses, and more especially to the latter of the two. We find the same paratactic construction in connection with other conjunctions (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.12">Isa 65:12</reference>). They were called upon to decide and answer as to this <hi type="italic">what</hi> and <hi type="italic">wherefore</hi>; but they were silent, just because they could clearly see that they would have to condemn themselves (as David condemned himself in connection with Nathan’s parable, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.5">2Sa 12:5</reference>). The Lord of the vineyard, therefore, begins to speak. He, its accuser, will now also be its judge.
entries.492cce4261b35b5542202009be5dbe9c480e3699: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa 5:5</reference> <hi type="italic">“Now then, I will tell you what I will do at once to my vineyard: take away its hedge, and it shall be for grazing; pull down its wall, and it shall be for treading down.”</hi> Before “now then” (<hi type="italic">vattâh</hi>) we must imagine a pause, as in Isa 3:14. The Lord of the vineyard breaks the silence of the umpires, which indicates their consciousness of guilt. They shall hear from Him what He will do at once to His vineyard (<hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">l'carmi</hi>, as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">“I will do:”</hi> <hi type="italic">ani</hi> <hi type="italic">'ōeh</hi>, <hi type="italic">fut. instans</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">facturus sum</hi> (Ges. §134, 2, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). In the <hi type="italic">inf. abs</hi>. which follow He opens up what He will do. On this explanatory use of the <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Isa 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference>-7. In such cases as these it takes the place of the object, as in other cases of the subject, but always in an abrupt manner (Ges. §131, 1). He would take away the <hi type="italic">mesucah</hi>, i.e., the green thorny hedge (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">Pro 15:19</reference>; Hos 2:8) with which the vineyard was enclosed, and would pull down the <hi type="italic">gârēd</hi>, i.e., the low stone wall (Num 22:24; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.31">Pro 24:31</reference>), which had been surrounded by the hedge of thorn-bushes to make a better defence, as well as for the protection of the wall itself, more especially against being undermined; so that the vineyard would be given up to grazing and treading down (lxx καταπα'τημα), i.e., would become an open way and gathering-place for man and beast.
entries.289c55be558586dfb0380a2fdb466176f9d4b64e: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Isa 5:6</reference> <div eID="gen12852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12853" type="x-p"/> This puts an end to the unthankful vineyard, and indeed a hopeless one.<hi type="italic">”And I will put an end to it: it shall not be pruned nor digged, and it shall break out in thorns and thistles; and I will command the clouds to rain no rain over it.”</hi> <hi type="italic">“Put an end:”</hi> <hi type="italic">bâthâh</hi> (= <hi type="italic">battâh</hi> : Ges. §67, Anm. 11) signifies, according to the primary meaning of <hi type="italic">bâthath</hi> (בּוּת, בּהת, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>), viz., <hi type="italic">abscindere</hi>, either <hi type="italic">abscissum</hi> = <hi type="italic">locus abscissus</hi> or <hi type="italic">praeruptus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.19">Isa 7:19</reference>), or <hi type="italic">abscissio</hi> = <hi type="italic">deletio</hi>. The latter is the meaning here, where <hi type="italic">shı̄th</hi> <hi type="italic">bâthâh</hi> is a refined expression for the more usual כלה עשׂה, both being construed with the accusative of the thing which is brought to an end. Further pruning and hoeing would do it no good, but only lead to further disappointment: it was the will of the Lord, therefore, that the deceitful vineyard should shoot up in thorns and thistles (<hi type="italic">âlâh</hi> is applied to the soil, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa 34:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.24.31">Pro 24:31</reference>; <hi type="italic">shâimr</hi> <hi type="italic">vâshaith</hi>, thorns and thistles, are in the accusative, according to Ges. §138, 1, Anm. 2; and both the words themselves, and also their combination, are exclusively and peculiarly Isaiah's).<note placement="foot">Cassel associates <hi type="italic">shâmir</hi> as the name of a plant (<hi type="italic">saxifraga</hi>) with σμὐρις, and <hi type="italic">shaith</hi> with <hi type="italic">sentis</hi>, ἄκανθα; but the name <hi type="italic">shâmir</hi> is not at all applicable to those small delicate plants, which are called <hi type="italic">saxifraga</hi> (stone-breakers) on account of their growing out of clefts in the rock, and so appearing to have split the rock itself. Both <hi type="italic">shâmir</hi> <hi type="italic">vâshaith</hi> and <hi type="italic">kōts</hi> <hi type="italic">v'dardar</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen 3:18</reference>, seem rather to point to certain kinds of <hi type="italic">rhamnus</hi>, together with different kinds of thistles. The more arid and waste the ground is, the more does it abound, where not altogether without vegetation, in thorny, prickly, stunted productions.</note> <div eID="gen12853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12854" type="x-p"/> In order that it might remain a wilderness, the clouds would also receive commandment from the Lord not to rain upon it. There can be no longer any doubt who the Lord of the vineyard is. He is Lord of the clouds, and therefore the Lord of heaven and earth. It is He who is the prophet’s beloved and dearest one. The song which opened in so minstrel-like and harmless a tone, has now become painfully severe and terribly repulsive. The husk of the parable, which has already been broken through, now falls completely off (cf., <reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">Mat 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">Mat 25:30</reference>). What it sets forth in symbol is really true. This truth the prophet establishes by an open declaration.
entries.4e866e5b5ca6db5ec20dcc3e78ba20962c80a696: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">Isa 5:7</reference> <hi type="italic">“For the vineyard of Jehovah of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plantation of His delight: He waited for justice, and behold grasping; for righteousness, and behold a shriek.”</hi> The meaning is not that the Lord of the vineyard would not let any more rain fall upon it, because this Lord was Jehovah (which is not affirmed in fact in the words commencing with “for,” <hi type="italic">Ci</hi>), but a more general one. This was how the case stood with the vineyard; for all Israel, and especially the people of Judah, were this vineyard, which had so bitterly deceived the expectations of its Lord, and indeed “the vineyard of Jehovah of hosts,” and therefore of the omnipotent God, whom even the clouds would serve when He came forth to punish. The expression “for” (<hi type="italic">Ci</hi>) is not only intended to vindicate the truth of the last statement, but the truth of the whole simile, including this: it is an explanatory “for” (<hi type="italic">Ci</hi> <hi type="italic">explic.</hi>), which opens the <hi type="italic">epimythion</hi>. “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts” (<hi type="italic">Cerem Jehovah Zebaoth</hi>) is the predicate. “The house of Israel (<hi type="italic">Beth Yisrâel</hi>) was the whole nation, which is also represented in other passages under the same figure of a vineyard (Isa 27:2.; Ps 80, etc.). But as Isaiah was prophet in Judah, he applies the figure more particularly to Judah, which was called Jehovah’s favourite plantation, inasmuch as it was the seat of the divine sanctuary and of the Davidic kingdom. This makes it easy enough to interpret the different parts of the simile employed. The fat mountain-horn was Canaan, flowing with milk and honey (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>); the digging of the vineyard, and clearing it of stones, was the clearing of Canaan from its former heathen inhabitants (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.3">Psa 54:3</reference>); the sorek-vines were the holy priests and prophets and kings of Israel of the earlier and better times (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer 2:21</reference>); the defensive and ornamental tower in the midst of the vineyard was Jerusalem as the royal city, with Zion the royal fortress (Mic 4:8); the winepress-trough was the temple, where, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference> (8.), the wine of heavenly pleasures flowed in streams, and from which, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference> and many other passages, the thirst of the soul might all be quenched. The grazing and treading down are explained in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">Jer 5:10</reference> and Jer 12:10. The bitter deception experienced by Jehovah is expressed in a play upon two words, indicating the surprising change of the desired result into the very opposite. The explanation which Gesenius, Caspari, Knobel, and others give of <hi type="italic">mispâch</hi>, viz., bloodshed, does not commend itself; for even if it must be admitted that <hi type="italic">sâphach</hi> occurs once or twice in the “Arabizing” book of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.30.7">Job 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job 14:19</reference>) in the sense of pouring out, this verbal root is strange to the Hebrew (and the Aramaean). Moreover, <hi type="italic">mispâch</hi> in any case would only mean pouring or shedding, and not bloodshed; and although the latter would certainly be possible by the side of the Arabic <hi type="italic">saffâch</hi>, <hi type="italic">saffâk</hi> (shedder of blood), yet it would be such an ellipsis as cannot be shown anywhere else in Hebrew usage. On the other hand, the rendering “leprosy” does not yield any appropriate sense, as <hi type="italic">mispachath</hi> (<hi type="italic">sappachath</hi>) is never generalized anywhere else into the single idea of “dirt” (Luzzatto: <hi type="italic">sozzura</hi>), nor does it appear as an ethical notion. We therefore prefer to connect it with a meaning unquestionably belonging to the verb ספח (see <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.36">1Sa 2:36</reference>; <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Isa 14:1</reference>; <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1Sa 26:19</reference>), which is derived in יסף, אסף, סוּף, from the primary notion “to sweep,” <hi type="italic">spec.</hi> to sweep towards, sweep in, or sweep away. Hence we regard <hi type="italic">mispach</hi> as denoting the forcible appropriation of another man’s property; certainly a suitable antithesis to <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi>. The prophet describes, in full-toned figures, how the expected noble grapes had turned into wild grapes, with nothing more than an outward resemblance. The introduction to the prophecy closes here. <div eID="gen12854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12855" type="x-p"/> The prophecy itself follows next, a seven-fold discourse composed of the six-fold woe contained in vv. 8-23, and the announcement of punishment in which it terminates. In this six-fold woe the prophet describes the bad fruits one by one. In confirmation of our rendering of <hi type="italic">mispâch</hi>, the first woe relates to covetousness and avarice as the root of all evil.
entries.309664e206007d7078f7b083b6e9fb9a13dd2a4d: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa 5:8</reference> <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that join house to house, who lay field to field, till there is no more room, and ye alone are dwelling in the midst of the land.”</hi> The participle is continued in the finite verb, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1">Isa 10:1</reference>; the regular syntactic construction is cases of this kind (Ges. §134, Anm. 2). The preterites after “till” (there are to such preterites, for <hi type="italic">'ephes</hi> is an intensified אין enclosing the verbal idea) correspond to future perfects: “They, the insatiable, would not rest till, after every smaller piece of landed property had been swallowed by them, the whole land had come into their possession, and no one beside themselves was settled in the land” (<reference osisRef="Job.22.8">Job 22:8</reference>). Such covetousness was all the more reprehensible, because the law of Israel and provided so very stringently and carefully, that as far as possible there should be an equal distribution of the soil, and that hereditary family property should be inalienable. All landed property that had been alienated reverted to the family every fiftieth year, or year of jubilee; so that alienation simply had reference to the usufruct of the land till that time. It was only in the case of houses in towns that the right of redemption was restricted to one year, at least according to a later statute. How badly the law of the year of jubilee had been observed, may be gathered from Jer 34, where we learn that the law as to the manumission of Hebrew slaves in the sabbatical year had fallen entirely into neglect. Isaiah’s contemporary, Micah, makes just the same complaint as Isaiah himself (vid., Mic 2:2).
entries.d5e8dd8316c2b26732645be19a25ab1a4c1dc7f2: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9-Isa.5.10">Isa 5:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen12855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12856" type="x-p"/> And the denunciation of punishment is made by him in very similar terms to those which we find here in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">Isa 5:10</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Into mine ears Jehovah of hosts: Of a truth many houses shall become a wilderness, great and beautiful ones deserted. For ten yokes of vineyard will yield one pailful, and a quarter of seed-corn will produce a bushel.”</hi> We may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Isa 22:14</reference> in what sense the prophet wrote the substantive clause, “Into mine ears,” or more literally, “In mine ears is <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> <hi type="italic">Zebaoth</hi>,” viz., He is here revealing Himself to me. In the pointing, בּאזני is written with <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi> as a pausal form, to indicate to the reader that the boldness of the expression is to be softened down by the assumption of an ellipsis. In Hebrew, “to say into the ears” did not mean to “speak softly and secretly,” as <reference osisRef="Gen.23.10">Gen 23:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.23.16">Gen 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.8">Job 33:8</reference>, and other passages, clearly show; but to speak in a distinct and intelligible manner, which precludes the possibility of any misunderstanding. The prophet, indeed, had not Jehovah standing locally beside him; nevertheless, he had Him objectively over against his own personality, and was well able to distinguish very clearly the thoughts and words of his own personality, from the words of Jehovah which arose audibly within him. These words informed him what would be the fate of the rich and insatiable landowners. “Of a truth:” אם־לא (if not) introduces an oath of an affirmative character (the complete formula is <hi type="italic">Chai</hi> <hi type="italic">ani</hi> <hi type="italic">'im</hi>-<hi type="italic">lo'</hi>, “as I live if not”), just as <hi type="italic">'im</hi> (if) alone introduces a negative oath (e.g., Num 14:23).
