The force of the expression <hi type="italic">'im</hi>-<hi type="italic">lo'</hi> extends not only to <hi type="italic">rabbim</hi>, as the false accentuation with <hi type="italic">gershayim</hi> (double-geresh) would make it appear, but to the whole of the following sentence, as it is correctly accentuated with rebia in the Venetian (1521) and other early editions. A universal desolation would ensue: <hi type="italic">rabbim</hi> (many) does not mean less than all; but the houses (<hi type="italic">bâttim</hi>, as the word should be pronounced, notwithstanding Ewald’s objection to Köhler’s remarks on Zec 14:2; cf., Job 2:1-13 :31) constituted altogether a very large number (compare the use of the word “many” in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mat 20:28</reference>, etc.). מאין is a double, and therefore an absolute, negation (so that there is not, no inhabitant, i.e., not any inhabitant at all). <reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">Isa 5:10</reference>, which commences, with <hi type="italic">Ci</hi>, explains how such a desolation of the houses would be brought about: failure of crops produces famine, and this is followed by depopulation. “<hi type="italic">Ten</hi> <hi type="italic">zimdē</hi> (with <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> <hi type="italic">lene</hi>, Ewald) <hi type="italic">of vineyard”</hi> are either ten pieces of the size that a man could plough in one day with a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> of oxen, or possibly ten portions of <hi type="italic">yoke</hi>-like espaliers of vines, i.e., of vines trained on cross laths (the <hi type="italic">vina jugata</hi> of Varro), which is the explanation adopted by Biesenthal. But if we compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.14">1Sa 14:14</reference>, the former is to be preferred, although the links are wanting which would enable us to prove that the early Israelites had one and the same system of land measure as the Romans;<note placement="foot">On the <hi type="italic">jugerum</hi>, see Hultsch, <hi type="italic">Griechische und römische Metrologie</hi>, 1862. The Greek <hi type="italic">plethron</hi>, which was smaller by two and a half, corresponded to some extent to this; also the Homeric <hi type="italic">tetraguon</hi>, which cannot be more precisely defined (according to Eustathius, it was a piece of land which a skilful labourer could plough in one day). According to Herod. ii. 168, in the Egyptian square-measure an <hi type="italic">a'roura</hi> was equal to 150 cubits square. The Palestinian, according to the tables of Julian the Ashkalonite, was the <hi type="italic">plethron</hi>. “The <hi type="italic">plethron</hi>,” he says, “was ten perches, or fifteen fathoms, or thirty paces, sixty cubits, ninety feet” (for the entire text, see L. F. V. Fennersberg’s <hi type="italic">Untersuchungen über alte Langen-, Feld-, und Wegemaase</hi>, 1859). Fennersberg’s conclusion is, that the <hi type="italic">tzemed</hi> was a <hi type="italic">plethron</hi>, equal in length to ten perches of nine feet each. But the meaning of the word <hi type="italic">tzemed</hi> is of more importance in helping to determine the measure referred to, than the tables of long measure of the architect of Ashkalon, which have been preserved in the imperial collection of laws of Constantine Harmenopulos, and which probably belong to a much later period.</note> nevertheless Arab. <hi type="italic">fddân</hi> (in Hauran) is precisely similar, and this word signifies primarily a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> of oxen, and then a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> (<hi type="italic">jugerum</hi>) regarded as a measure of land. Ten days’ work would only yield a single <hi type="italic">bath</hi>. This liquid measure, which was first introduced in the time of the kings, corresponded to the <hi type="italic">ephah</hi> in dry measure (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.11">Eze 45:11</reference>). According to Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 2, 9), it was equal to seventy-two Roman <hi type="italic">sextarii</hi>, i.e., a little more than thirty-three Berlin quarts; but in the time of Isaiah it was probably smaller. The <hi type="italic">homer</hi>, a dry measure, generally called a <hi type="italic">Cor</hi> after the time of the kings, was equal to ten Attic <hi type="italic">medimnoi</hi>;<note placement="foot">Or rather 7 1/2 Attic <hi type="italic">medimnoi</hi> = 10 Attic <hi type="italic">metretoi</hi> = 45 Roman <hi type="italic">modia</hi> (see Böckh, <hi type="italic">Metrologische Untersuchungen</hi>, p. 259).</note> a <hi type="italic">medimnos</hi> being (according to Josephus, <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xv 9, 2) about 15-16ths of a Berlin bushel, and therefore a little more than fifteen pecks. Even if this quantity of corn should be sown, they would not reap more than an <hi type="italic">ephah</hi>.The harvest, therefore, would only yield the tenth part of the sowing, since an <hi type="italic">ephah</hi> was the tenth part of a <hi type="italic">homer</hi>, or three <hi type="italic">seahs</hi>, the usual minimum for one baking (vid., <reference osisRef="Matt.13.33">Mat 13:33</reference>). It is, of course, impossible to give the relative measure exactly in our translation.
entries.a7241e788d2ba6455231252e4735df0485709380: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference> <div eID="gen12856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12857" type="x-p"/> The second woe, for which the curse about to fall upon vinedressing (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.5.10">Isa 5:10</reference></hi>) prepared the way by the simple association of ideas, is directed against the debauchees, who in their carnal security carried on their excesses even in the daylight. <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning to run after strong drink; who continue till late at night with wine inflaming them!”</hi> <hi type="italic">Boker</hi> (from <hi type="italic">bâkar</hi>, <hi type="italic">bakara</hi>, to slit, to tear up, or split) is the break of day; and <hi type="italic">nesheph</hi> (from <hi type="italic">nâshaph</hi>, to blow) the cool of the evening, including the night (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.4">Isa 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Isa 59:10</reference>); <hi type="italic">'ichër</hi>, to continue till late, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.23.30">Pro 23:30</reference> : the construct state before words with a preposition, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>, and many other passages (Ges. §116, 1). <hi type="italic">Shēcâr</hi>, in connection with <hi type="italic">yayin</hi>, is the general name for every other kind of strong drink, more especially for wines made artificially from fruit, honey, raisins, dates, etc., including barley-wine (οἶνος κρίθινος) or beer (ἐκ κριθῶν μέθυ in Aeschylus, also called βρῦτον βρυτόν ζῦθος ζύθος, and by many other names), a beverage known in Egypt, which was half a wine country and half a beer country, from as far back as the time of the Pharaohs. The form <hi type="italic">shēcâr</hi> is composed, like ענב (with the fore-tone <hi type="italic">tsere</hi>), from <hi type="italic">shâcar</hi>, to intoxicate; according to the Arabic, literally to close by stopping up, i.e., to stupefy.<note placement="foot">It is a question, therefore, whether the name of sugar is related to it or not. The Arabic <hi type="italic">sakar</hi> corresponds to the Hebrew <hi type="italic">shecâr</hi>; but sugar is called <hi type="italic">sukkar</hi>, Pers. <hi type="italic">'sakkar</hi>, <hi type="italic">'sakar</hi>, no doubt equivalent to σἀκχαρι (Arrian in <hi type="italic">Periplus</hi>, μἐλι τὸ καλἀμινον τὸ λεγὀμενου σἀκχαρι), <hi type="italic">saccharum</hi>, an Indian word, which is pronounced <hi type="italic">Carkarâ</hi> in Sanscrit and <hi type="italic">sakkara</hi> in Prakrit, and signifies “forming broken pieces,” i.e., sugar in grains or small lumps (brown sugar). The art of boiling sugar from the cane was an Indian invention (see Lassen, <hi type="italic">Indische Alterthumskunde</hi>, i. 269ff.). The early Egyptian name for beer is <hi type="italic">hek</hi> (Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Recueil</hi>, p. 118); the demotic and hieratic name <hi type="italic">henk</hi>, the Coptic <hi type="italic">henke</hi>. The word ζῦθος ζὐθος) is also old Egyptian. In the <hi type="italic">Book of the Dead</hi> (79, 8) the deceased says, “I have taken sacrificial cakes from the table, I have drunk <hi type="italic">seth - t</hi> in the evening.” Moses Stuart wrote an <hi type="italic">Essay upon the Wines and Strong Drinks of the Ancient Hebrews</hi>, which was published in London (1831), with a preface by J. Pye Smith.</note> <div eID="gen12857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12858" type="x-p"/> The clauses after the two participles are circumstantial clauses (Ewald, §341, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), indicating the circumstances under which they ran out so early, and sat till long after dark: they hunted after mead, they heated themselves with wine, namely, to drown the consciousness of their deeds of darkness. <div eID="gen12858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12859" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference> describes how they go on in their blindness with music and carousing: <hi type="italic">“And guitar and harp, kettle-drum, and flute, and wine, is their feast; but they regard not the work of Jehovah, and see not the purpose of His hands.”</hi> <hi type="italic">“Their feast”</hi> is so and so (משׁתּיהם is only a plural in appearance; it is really a singular, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.10">Dan 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.16">Dan 1:16</reference>, and many other passages, with the <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> of the primary form, משׁתּי = משׁתּה, softened: see the remarks on עלה at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.30">Isa 1:30</reference>, and עשׂיה at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>); that is to say, their feast consisted or was composed of exciting music and wine. Knobel construes it, “and there are guitar, etc., and wine is their drink;” but a divided sentence of this kind is very tame; and the other expression, based upon the general principle, “The whole is its parts,” is thoroughly Semitic (see Fleischer’s <hi type="italic">Abhandlungen über einige Arten der Nominalapposition in den Sitzungsberichten der sächs</hi>. <hi type="italic">Gesellschaft der Wissenschaft</hi>, 1862). <hi type="italic">Cinnor</hi> (guitar) is a general name for such instruments as have their strings drawn (upon a bridge) over a sounding board; and <hi type="italic">nebel</hi> (the harp and lyre) a general name for instruments with their strings hung freely, so as to be played with both hands at the same time. <hi type="italic">Toph</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">duff</hi>) is a general name for the tambourin, the drum, and the kettle-drum; <hi type="italic">Chaill</hi> (lit. that which is bored through) a general name for the flute and double flute. In this tumult and riot they had no thought or eye for the work of Jehovah and the purpose of His hands. This is the phrase used to express the idea of eternal counsel of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>), which leads to salvation by the circuitous paths of judgment (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">Isa 29:23</reference>), so far as that counsel is embodied in history, as moulded by the invisible interposition of God. In their joy and glory they had no sense for what was the most glorious of all, viz., the moving and working of God in history; so that they could not even discern the judgment which was in course of preparation at that very time.
entries.cae5964a9f881dff2b3547f92bca5212d4053478: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Isa 5:13</reference> <div eID="gen12859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12860" type="x-p"/> Therefore judgment would overtake them in this blind, dull, and stupid animal condition. <hi type="italic">“Therefore my people go into banishment without knowing; and their glory will become starving men, and their tumult men dried up with thirst.”</hi> As the word <hi type="italic">“therefore”</hi> (<hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa 1:24</reference>) introduces the threat of punishment, <hi type="italic">gâlâh</hi> (go into captivity) is a prophetic preterite. Israel would go into exile, and that “without knowing” (<hi type="italic">mibb'li</hi>-<hi type="italic">da'ath</hi>). The meaning of this expression cannot be “from want of knowledge,” since the <hi type="italic">min</hi> which is fused into one word with <hi type="italic">b'li</hi> is not causal, but negative, and <hi type="italic">mibb'li</hi>, as a preposition, always signifies “without” (<hi type="italic">absque</hi>). But are we to render it “without knowing it” (as in Hos 4:6, where <hi type="italic">hadda'ath</hi> has the article), or “unawares?” There is no necessity for any dispute on this point, since the two renderings are fundamentally one and the same. The knowledge, of which <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference> pronounces them destitute, was more especially a knowledge of the judgment of God that was hanging over them; so that, as the captivity would come upon them without knowledge, it would necessarily come upon them unawares. “Their glory” (<hi type="italic">Cebōdō</hi>) and <hi type="italic">“their tumult”</hi> (<hi type="italic">hamono</hi>) are therefore to be understood, as the predicates show, as collective nouns used in a personal sense, the former signifying the more select portion of the nation (cf., Mic 1:15), the latter the mass of the people, who were living in rioting and tumult. The former would become <hi type="italic">“men of famine”</hi> (<hi type="italic">mĕthē</hi> <hi type="italic">rââb</hi>: מתי, like אנשׁי in other places, viz., <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">2Sa 19:29</reference>, or בּני, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.16">1Sa 26:16</reference>); the latter <hi type="italic">“men dried up with thirst”</hi> (<hi type="italic">tsichēh</hi> <hi type="italic">tsâmâh</hi>: the same number as the subject). There is no necessity to read מתי (dead men) instead of מתי, as the lxx and Vulgate do, or מזי (מזה) according to <reference osisRef="Deut.32.24">Deu 32:24</reference>, as Hitzig, Ewald, Böttcher, and others propose (compare, on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>). The adjective <hi type="italic">tzicheh</hi> (<hi type="italic">hapax</hi> <hi type="italic">leg</hi>) is formed like <hi type="italic">Chirēsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">Cēheh</hi>, and other adjectives which indicate defects: in such formations from verbs <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> - <hi type="italic">He</hi>, instead of <hi type="italic">e</hi> we have an <hi type="italic">ae</hi> that has grown out of <hi type="italic">ay</hi> (Olshausen, §182, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The rich gluttons would starve, and the tippling crowd would die with thirst.
entries.704ac440a8ae5edd734bac7faca274b6ea8634a6: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference> <div eID="gen12860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12861" type="x-p"/> The threat of punishment commences again with “therefore;” it has not yet satisfied itself, and therefore grasps deeper still. <hi type="italic">“Therefore the under-world opens its jaws wide, and stretches open its mouth immeasurably wide; and the glory of Jerusalem descends, and its tumult, and noise, and those who rejoice within it.”</hi> The verbs which follow <hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi> (therefore) are prophetic preterites, as in Isa 5:13. The feminine suffixes attached to what the lower world swallows up do not refer to <hi type="italic">sheol</hi> (though this is construed more frequently, no doubt, as a feminine than as a masculine, as it is in <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job 26:6</reference>), but, as expressed in the translation, to Jerusalem itself, which is also necessarily required by the last clause, “those who rejoice within it.” The withdrawal of the tone from ועלז to the penultimate (cf., <hi type="italic">Châphētz</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">Psa 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>) is intentionally omitted, to cause the rolling and swallowing up to be heard as it were. A mouth is ascribed to the under-world, also a <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi>, i.e., a greedy soul, in which sense <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi> is then applied metonymically sometimes to a thirst for blood (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">Psa 27:12</reference>), and sometimes to simple greediness (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Isa 56:11</reference>), and even, as in the present passage and <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>, to the throat or swallow which the soul opens “without measure,” when its craving knows no bounds (<hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 204). It has become a common thing now to drop entirely the notion which formerly prevailed, that the noun <hi type="italic">sheol</hi> was derived from the verb <hi type="italic">shâal</hi> in the sense in which it was generally employed, viz., to ask or demand; but Caspari, who has revived it again, is certainly so far correct, that the derivation of the word which the prophet had in his mind was this and no other. The word <hi type="italic">sheol</hi> (an infinitive form, like <hi type="italic">pekōd</hi>) signifies primarily the irresistible and inexorable demand made upon every earthly thing; and then secondarily, in a local sense, the place of the abode of shades, to which everything on the surface of the earth is summoned; or essentially the divinely appointed curse which demands and swallows up everything upon the earth. We simply maintain, however, that the word <hi type="italic">sheol</hi>, as generally sued, was associated in thought with <hi type="italic">shâal</hi>, to ask or demand. Originally, no doubt, it may have been derived from the primary and more material idea of the verb שׁאל, possibly from the meaning “to be hollow,” which is also assumed to be the primary meaning of שׁעל.<note placement="foot">The meaning “to be hollow” is not very firmly established, however; as the primary meaning of שׁעל, and the analogy sometimes adduced of hell = hollow (Hölle = Höhle), is a deceptive one, as Hölle (hell), to which Luther always gives the more correct form Helle, does not mean a hollow, but a hidden place (or a place which renders invisible: from <hi type="italic">hëln</hi>, to conceal), Lat. <hi type="italic">celans</hi> (see Jütting, Bibl. Wörterbuch, 1864, pp. 85, 86). It is much more probable that the meaning of sheol is not the hollow place, but the depression or depth, from של, which corresponds precisely to the Greek χαλᾶν so far as its primary meaning is concerned (compare the <hi type="italic">talmud</hi>ic <hi type="italic">shilshêl</hi>, to let down; <hi type="italic">shilshul</hi>, sinking or depression, Erubin 83b; <hi type="italic">shul</hi>, the foundation, fundus): see Hupfeld on Psa 6:6. Luzzatto on this passage also explains sheol as signifying depth, and compares the talmudic <hi type="italic">hishchil</hi> = <hi type="italic">hēshil</hi>, to let down (or, according to others, to draw up - two meanings which may easily be combined in the same word, starting from its radical idea, which indicates in a general a loosening of the previous connection). Fürst has also given up the meaning cavitas, a hollow, and endeavours to find a more correct explanation of the primary signification of <hi type="italic">shâ'al</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa 40:12</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen12861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12862" type="x-p"/> At any rate, this derivation answers to the view that generally prevailed in ancient times. According to the prevalent idea, Hades was in the interior of the earth. And there was nothing really absurd in this, since it is quite within the power and freedom of the omnipresent God to manifest Himself wherever and however He may please. As He reveals Himself above the earth, i.e., in heaven, among blessed spirits in the light of His love; so did He reveal Himself underneath the earth, viz., in <hi type="italic">Sheōl</hi>, in the darkness and fire of His wrath. And with the exception of Enoch and Elijah, with their marvellous departure from this life, the way of every mortal ended there, until the time when Jesus Christ, having first paid the λὐτρον, i.e., having shed His blood, which covers our guilt and turns the wrath of God into love, descended into Hades and ascended into heaven, and from that time forth has changed the death of all believers from a descent into Hades into an ascension to heaven. But even under the Old Testament the believer may have known, that whoever hid himself on this side the grave in Jehovah the living One, would retain his eternal germ of life even in <hi type="italic">Sheōl</hi> in the midst of the shades, and would taste the love of God even in the midst of wrath. It was this postulate of faith which lay at the foundation of the fact, that even under the Old Testament the broader and more comprehensive idea of <hi type="italic">Sheōl</hi> began to be contracted into the more limited notion of hell (see <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 415). This is the case in the passage before us, where Isaiah predicts of everything of which Jerusalem was proud, and in which it revelled, including the persons who rejoice din these things, a descent into Hades; just as the Korahite author of Ps 49 wrote (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>) that the beauty of the wicked would be given up to Hades to be consumed, without having hereafter any place in the upper world, when the upright should have dominion over them in the morning. Hades even here is almost equivalent to the New Testament <hi type="italic">gehenna</hi>.
entries.41517344226a2237a3e412127033c177fcdd5467: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.15-Isa.5.16">Isa 5:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen12862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12863" type="x-p"/> The prophet now repeats a thought which formed one of the refrains of the second prophetic address (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">Isa 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">Isa 2:17</reference>). It acquires here a still deeper sense, from the context in which it stands. <hi type="italic">“Then are mean men bowed down, and lords humbled, and the eyes of lofty men are humbled. And Jehovah of hosts shows Himself exalted in judgment, and God the Holy One sanctifies Himself in righteousness.”</hi> That which had exalted itself from earth to heaven, would be cast down earthwards into hell. The consecutive futures depict the coming events, which are here represented as historically present, as the direct sequel of what is also represented as present in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference> : Hades opens, and then both low and lofty in Jerusalem sink down, and the soaring eyes now wander about in horrible depths. God, who is both exalted and holy in Himself, demanded that as the exalted One He should be exalted, and that as the Holy One He should be sanctified. But Jerusalem had not done that; He would therefore prove Himself the exalted One by the execution of justice, and sanctify Himself (<hi type="italic">nikdash</hi> is to be rendered as a reflective verb, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.23">Eze 36:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.23">Eze 38:23</reference>) by the manifestation of righteousness, in consequence of which the people of Jerusalem would have to give Him glory against their will, as forming part of “the things under the earth” (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Phi 2:10</reference>). Jerusalem has been swallowed up twice in this manner by Hades; once in the Chaldean war, and again in the Roman. But the invisible background of these outward events was the fact, that it had already fallen under the power of hell. And now, even in a more literal sense, ancient Jerusalem, like the company of Korah (Num 16:30, Num 16:33), has gone underground. Just as Babylon and Nineveh, the ruins of which are dug out of the inexhaustible mine of their far-stretching foundation and soil, have sunk beneath the ground; so do men walk about in modern Jerusalem over the ancient Jerusalem, which lies buried beneath; and many an enigma of topography will remain an enigma until ancient Jerusalem has been dug out of the earth again.
entries.a00d5ba3bb1562cbf83d3583cdaa4fbc4dcb9c7a: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Isa 5:17</reference> <div eID="gen12863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12864" type="x-p"/> And when we consider that the Holy Land is at the present time an extensive pasture-ground for Arab shepherds, and that the modern Jerusalem which has arisen from the dust is a Mohammedan city, we may see in this also a literal fulfilment of <reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Isa 5:17</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And lambs feed as upon their pasture, and nomad shepherds eat the waste places of the fat ones.”</hi> There is no necessity to supply an object to the verb ורעוּ, as Knobel and others assume, viz., the waste lands mentioned in the second clause; nor is <hi type="italic">Cedâbrâm</hi> to be taken as the object, as Caspari supposes; but the place referred to is determined by the context: in the place where Jerusalem is sunken, there lambs feed after the manner of their own pasture-ground, i.e., just as if they were in their old accustomed pasture (<hi type="italic">dober</hi>, as in Mic 2:12, from <hi type="italic">dâbar</hi>, to drive). The lambs intended are those of the <hi type="italic">gârim</hi> mentioned in the second clause. The <hi type="italic">gârim</hi> themselves are men leading an unsettled, nomad, or pilgrim life; as distinguished from <hi type="italic">gêrim</hi>, strangers visiting, or even settled at a place. The lxx have ἄρνες, so that they must have read either <hi type="italic">Cârim</hi> or <hi type="italic">gedâim</hi>, which Ewald, Knobel, and others adopt. But one feature of the prophecy, which is sustained by the historical fulfilment, is thereby obliterated. <hi type="italic">Chârboth</hi> <hi type="italic">mêchim</hi> are the lands of those that were formerly marrowy, i.e., fat and strutting about in their fulness; which lands had now become waste places. Knobel’s statement, that <hi type="italic">âcăl</hi> is out of place in connection with <hi type="italic">gârim</hi>, is overthrown by <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7">Isa 1:7</reference>, to which he himself refers, though he makes he-goats the subject instead of men. The second woe closes with Isa 5:17. It is the longest of all. This also serves to confirm the fact that luxury was the leading vice of Judah in the time of Uzziah-Jotham, as it was that of Israel under Jeroboam II (see <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.14">Amo 6:1-14</reference>, where the same threat is held out).
entries.338ce64df3f3eb08394b18f4862f9f58820d6da3: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.18">Isa 5:18</reference> <div eID="gen12864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12865" type="x-p"/> The third woe is directed against the supposed strong-minded men, who called down the judgment of God by presumptuous sins and wicked words. <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that draw crime with cords of lying, and sin as with the rope of the waggon.”</hi> Knobel and most other commentators take <hi type="italic">mâshak</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">attrahere</hi> (to draw towards one’s self): “They draw towards them sinful deeds with cords of lying palliation, and the cart-rope of the most daring presumption;” and cite, as parallel examples, <reference osisRef="Job.40.24">Job 40:24</reference> and Hos 11:4. But as <hi type="italic">mâshak</hi> is also used in <reference osisRef="Deut.21.3">Deu 21:3</reference> in the sense of drawing in a yoke, that is to say, drawing a plough or chariot; and as the waggon or cart (<hi type="italic">agâlâh</hi>, the word commonly used for a transport-waggon, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">mercâbâh</hi>, the state carriage or war chariot is expressly mentioned here, the figure employed is certainly the same as that which underlies the New Testament ἑτεροζυγεῖν (“unequally yoked,” <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.14">2Co 6:14</reference>). Iniquity was the burden which they drew after them with cords of lying (<hi type="italic">shâv'h</hi> : see at <reference osisRef="Ps.26.4">Psa 26:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.15.31">Job 15:31</reference>), i.e., “want of character or religion;” and sin was the waggon to which they were harnessed as if with a thick cart-rope (Hofmann, Drechsler, and Caspari; see Ewald, §221,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). Iniquity and sin are mentioned here as carrying with them their own punishment. The definite העון (crime or misdeed) is generic, and the indefinite הטּאה qualitative and massive. There is a bitter sarcasm involved in the bold figure employed. They were proud of their unbelief; but this unbelief was like a halter with which, like beasts of burden, they were harnessed to sin, and therefore to the punishment of sin, which they went on drawing further and further, in utter ignorance of the waggon behind them. <div eID="gen12865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12866" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference> shows very clearly that the prophet referred to the free-thinkers of his time, the persons who are called fools (<hi type="italic">nabal</hi>) and scorners (<hi type="italic">lētz</hi>) in the Psalms and Proverbs. <hi type="italic">“Who say, Let Him hasten, accelerate His work, that we may see; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may experience it.”</hi> They doubted whether the day of Jehovah would ever come (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.12-Jer.5.13">Jer 5:12-13</reference>), and went so far in their unbelief as to call out for what they could not and would not believe, and desired it to come that they might see it with their own eyes and experience it for themselves (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.15">Jer 17:15</reference>; it is different in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Amo 5:18</reference> and Mal 2:17-3:1, where this desire does not arise from scorn and defiance, but from impatience and weakness of faith). As the two verbs denoting haste are used both transitively and intransitively (vid., Jdg 20:37, to hasten or make haste), we might render the passage “let His work make haste,” as Hitzig, Ewald, Umbreit, and Drechsler do; but we prefer the rendering adopted by Gesenius, Caspari, and Knobel, on the basis of <reference osisRef="Isa.60.22">Isa 60:22</reference>, and take the verb as transitive, and Jehovah as the subject. The forms <hi type="italic">yâchishâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">taboâh</hi> are, with <reference osisRef="Ps.20.4">Psa 20:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>, probably the only examples of the expression of a wish in the third person, strengthened by the <hi type="italic">âh</hi>, which indicates a summons or appeal; for <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.20">Eze 23:20</reference>, which Gesenius cites (§48, 3), and <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>, to which Knobel refers, have no connection with this, as in both passages the <hi type="italic">âh</hi> is the feminine termination, and not hortative (vid., <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>, note, and at <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>). The fact that the free-thinkers called God “the Holy One of Israel,” whereas they scoffed at His intended final and practical attestation of Himself as the Holy One, may be explained from <reference osisRef="Isa.30.11">Isa 30:11</reference> : they took this name of God from the lips of the prophet himself, so that their scorn affected both God and His prophet at the same time.
entries.3b481cdefb7d4fcfcbddb3ca08603e3058be5fce: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Isa 5:20</reference> <div eID="gen12866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12867" type="x-p"/> The fourth woe: <hi type="italic">“Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who give out darkness for light, and light for darkness; who give out bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter.”</hi> The previous woe had reference to those who made the facts of sacred history the butt of their naturalistic doubt and ridicule, especially so far as they were the subject of prophecy. This fourth woe relates to those who adopted a code of morals that completely overturned the first principles of ethics, and was utterly opposed to the law of God; for evil, darkness, and bitter, with their respective antitheses, represent moral principles that are essentially related (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.23">Mat 6:23</reference>; Jam 3:11), Evil, as hostile to God, is dark in its nature, and therefore loves darkness, and is exposed to the punitive power of darkness. And although it may be sweet to the material taste, it is nevertheless bitter, inasmuch as it produces abhorrence and disgust in the godlike nature of man, and, after a brief period of self-deception, is turned into the bitter woe of fatal results. Darkness and light, bitter and sweet, therefore, are not tautological metaphors for evil and good; but epithets applied to evil and good according to their essential principles, and their necessary and internal effects.
entries.d24adf7ce7d0c035eeac3e28167d190276e21098: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.21">Isa 5:21</reference> <div eID="gen12867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12868" type="x-p"/> The fifth woe: <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight.”</hi> The third woe had reference to the unbelieving naturalists, the opponents of prophecy (<hi type="italic">nebuâh</hi>); the fourth to the moralists, who threw all into confusion; and to this there is appended, by a very natural association of ideas, the woe denounced upon those whom want of humility rendered inaccessible to that wisdom which went hand in hand with prophecy, and the true foundation of which was the fear of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ecc 12:13</reference>). <hi type="italic">“Be not wise in thine own eyes,”</hi> is a fundamental rule of this wisdom (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.7">Pro 3:7</reference>). It was upon this wisdom that that prophetic policy rested, whose warnings, as we read in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9-Isa.28.10">Isa 28:9-10</reference>, they so scornfully rejected. The next woe, which has reference to the administration of justice in the state, shows very clearly that in this woe the prophet had more especially the want of theocratic wisdom in relation to the affairs of state in his mind.
entries.b7300169f3ed97ca205e08207c85f679114eefa0: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22-Isa.5.23">Isa 5:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen12868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12869" type="x-p"/> The sixth woe: <hi type="italic">“Woe to those who are heroes to drink wine, and brave men to mix strong drink; who acquit criminals for a bribe, and take away from every one the righteousness of the righteous.”</hi> We see from <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference> that the drinkers in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference> are unjust judges. The threat denounced against these is Isaiah’s universal ceterum censeo; and accordingly it forms, in this instance also, the substance of his sixth and last woe. They are heroes; not, however, in avenging wrong, but in drinking wine; they are men of renown, though not for deciding between guilt and innocence, but for mixing up the ingredients of strong artistic wines. For the terms applied to such mixed wines, see <reference osisRef="Ps.75.9">Psa 75:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.30">Pro 23:30</reference>, Sol 7:3. It must be borne in mind, however, that what is here called <hi type="italic">shecâr</hi> was not, properly speaking, wine, but an artificial mixture, like date wine and cider. For such things as these they were noteworthy and strong; whereas they judged unjustly, and took bribes that they might consume the reward of their injustice in drink and debauchery (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7-Isa.28.8">Isa 28:7-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Pro 31:5</reference>). “For reward:” <hi type="italic">ēkeb</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ukb</hi>; different from <hi type="italic">âkēb</hi>, a heel, = <hi type="italic">‛akib</hi>) is an adverbial accusative, “in recompense,” or “for pay.” “<hi type="italic">From him</hi>” (<hi type="italic">mimmennu</hi>) is distributive, and refers back to <hi type="italic">tsaddikim</hi> (the righteous); as, for example, in Hos 4:8.
entries.5e7b1e764b5a61155c690181fc53afcffb51c085: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference> <div eID="gen12869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12870" type="x-p"/> In the three exclamations in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.18-Isa.5.21">Isa 5:18-21</reference>, Jehovah rested contented with the simple undeveloped “woe” (<hi type="italic">hoi</hi>). On the other hand, the first two utterances respecting the covetous and the debauchees were expanded into an elaborate denunciation of punishment. But now that the prophet has come to the unjust judges, the denunciation of punishment bursts out with such violence, that a return to the simple exclamation of “woe” is not to be thought of. The two “therefores” in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Isa 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>, a third is now added in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble, and hay sinks together in the flame, their root will become like mould, and their blossom fly up like dust; for they have despised the law of Jehovah of hosts, and scornfully rejected the proclamation of the Holy One of Israel.”</hi> The persons primarily intended as those described in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>, but with a further extension of the range of vision to Judah and Jerusalem, the vineyard of which they are the bad fruit. The sinners are compared to a plant which moulders into dust both above and below, i.e., altogether (cf., Mal 4:1, and the expression, “Let there be to him neither root below nor branch above,” in the inscription upon the sarcophagus of the Phoenician king <hi type="italic">Es'mun'azar</hi>). Their root moulders in the earth, and their blossom (<hi type="italic">perach</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.5">Isa 18:5</reference>) turns to fine dust, which the wind carries away. And this change in root and blossom takes place suddenly, as if through the force of fire. In the expression <hi type="italic">Ce'ecol kash leshon 'ēsh</hi> (“as the tongue of fire devours stubble”), which consists of four short words with three sibilant letters, we hear, as it were, the hissing of the flame. When the infinitive construct is connected with both subject and object, the subject generally stands first, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference>; but here the object is placed first, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Isa 20:1</reference> (Ges. §133, 3; Ewald, §307). In the second clause, the infinitive construct passes over into the finite verb, just as in the similarly constructed passage in Isa 64:1. As <hi type="italic">yirpeh</hi> has the intransitive meaning <hi type="italic">Collabi</hi>, to sink together, or collapse; either <hi type="italic">lehâbâh</hi> must be an <hi type="italic">acc. loci</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Chashash</hi> <hi type="italic">lehâbâh</hi> the construct state, signifying flame-hay, i.e., hay destined to the flame, or ascending in flame.<note placement="foot">In Arabic also, <hi type="italic">Chashı̄sh</hi> signifies hay; but in common usage (at least in Syriac) it is applied not to dried grass, but to green grass or barley: hence the expression <hi type="italic">yachush</hi> there is green fodder. Here, however, in Isaiah, <hi type="italic">Chashash</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">Chashish yâbis</hi>, and this is its true etymological meaning (see the Lexicons). But <hi type="italic">kash</hi> is still used in Syro-Arabic, to signify not stubble, but wheat that has been cut and is not yet threshed; whereas the radical word itself signifies to be dry, and <hi type="italic">Châshash</hi> consequently is used for mown grass, and <hi type="italic">kash</hi> for the dry halm of wheat, whether as stubble left standing in the ground, or as straw (vid., <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.39.13-Job.39.18">Job 39:13-18</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen12870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12871" type="x-p"/> As the reason for the sudden dissolution of the plantation of Judah, instead of certain definite sins being mentioned, the sin of all sins is given at once, namely, the rejection of the word of God with the heart (<hi type="italic">mâ'as</hi>), and in word and deed (<hi type="italic">ni'ēts</hi>). The double <hi type="italic">'ēth</hi> (with <hi type="italic">yethib</hi> immediately before <hi type="italic">pashta</hi>, as in eleven passages in all; see Heidenheim’s <hi type="italic">Imspete hate'amim</hi>, p. 20) and <hi type="italic">v'êth</hi> (with <hi type="italic">tebir</hi>) give prominence to the object; and the interchange of Jehovah of hosts with the Holy One of Israel makes the sin appear all the greater on account of the exaltation and holiness of God, who revealed Himself in this word, and indeed had manifested Himself to Israel as His own peculiar people. The prophet no sooner mentions the great sin of Judah, than the announcement of punishment receives, as it were, fresh fuel, and bursts out again.
entries.960d7f8136cc4ef373db999bf0d5b860fba99e72: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference> <hi type="italic">“Therefore is the wrath of Jehovah kindled against His people, and He stretches His hand over them, and smites them; then the hills tremble, and their carcases become like sweepings in the midst of the streets. For all this His anger is not appeased, and His hand is stretched out still.”</hi> We may see from these last words, which are repeated as a refrain in the cycle of prophecies relating to the time of Ahaz (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Isa 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">Isa 10:4</reference>), that the prophet had before his mind a distinct and complete judgment upon Judah, belonging to the immediate future. It was certainly a coming judgment, not one already past; for the verbs after “therefore” (<hi type="italic">‛al - cên</hi>), like those after the three previous <hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi>, are all prophetic preterites. It is impossible, therefore, to take the words “and the hills tremble” as referring to the earthquake in the time of Uzziah (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Amo 1:1</reference>; Zec 14:5). This judgment, which was closer at hand, would consist in the fact that Jehovah would stretch out His hand in His wrath over His people (or, as it is expressed elsewhere, would swing His hand: Luther, “wave His hand,” i.e., move it to and fro; vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Isa 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Isa 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Isa 30:32</reference>), and bring it down upon Judah with one stroke, the violence of which would be felt not only by men, but by surrounding nature as well. What kind of stroke this would be, was to be inferred from the circumstance that the corpses would lie unburied in the streets, like common street-sweepings. The reading תּצּות must be rejected. Early editors read the word much more correctly תּצּות; Buxtorf (1618) even adopts the reading תוּצות, which has the Masoretic pointing in Num 22:39 in its favour. It is very natural to connect <hi type="italic">Cassuchâh</hi> with the Arabic <hi type="italic">kusâcha</hi> (sweepings; see at <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Isa 33:12</reference>): but <hi type="italic">kusâc</hi> is the common form for waste or rubbish of this kind (e.g., <hi type="italic">kulâm</hi>, nail-cuttings), whereas <hi type="italic">Cassuach</hi> is a form which, like the forms <hi type="italic">fâōl</hi> (e.g., <hi type="italic">Châmōts</hi>) and <hi type="italic">fâūl</hi> (compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">fâsūs</hi>, a wind-maker, or wind-bag, i.e., a boaster), has always an intensive, active (e.g., <hi type="italic">Channun</hi>), or circumstantial signification (like <hi type="italic">shaccul</hi>), but is never found in a passive sense. The <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> is consequently to be taken as a particle of comparison (followed, as is generally the case, with a definite article); and <hi type="italic">sūchâh</hi> is to be derived from <hi type="italic">sūach</hi> (= <hi type="italic">verrere</hi>, to sweep). The reference, therefore, is not to a pestilence (which is designated, as a stroke from God, not by <hi type="italic">hiccâh</hi>, but by <hi type="italic">nâgaph</hi> ), but to the slaughter of battle; and if we look at the other terrible judgment threatened in Isa 5:26., which was to proceed from the imperial power, there can be no doubt that the spirit of prophecy here points to the massacre that took place in Judah in connection with the Syro-Ephraimitish war (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.5-2Chr.28.6">2Ch 28:5-6</reference>). The mountains may then have trembled with the marching of troops, and the din of arms, and the felling of trees, and the shout of war. At any rate, nature had to participate in what men had brought upon themselves; for, according to the creative appointment of God, nature bears the same relation to man as the body to the soul. Every stroke of divine wrath which falls upon a nation equally affects the land which has grown up, as it were, with it; and in this sense the mountains of Judah trembled at the time referred to, even though the trembling was only discernible by initiated ears. But “for all this” (<hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, = “notwithstanding,” “in spite of,” as in <reference osisRef="Job.1.22">Job 1:22</reference>) the wrath of Jehovah, as the prophet foresaw, would not turn away, as it was accustomed to do when He was satisfied; and His hand would still remain stretched out over Judah, ready to strike again.
entries.75142603a975d15300295150add4652c60065316: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Isa 5:26</reference> <div eID="gen12871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12872" type="x-p"/> Jehovah finds the human instruments of His further strokes, not in Israel and the neighbouring nations, but in the people of distant lands. <hi type="italic">“And lifts up a banner to the distant nations, and hisses to it from the end of the earth; and, behold, it comes with haste swiftly.”</hi> What the prophet here foretold began to be fulfilled in the time of Ahaz. But the prophecy, which commences with this verse, has every possible mark of the very opposite of a <hi type="italic">vaticinium post eventum</hi>. It is, strictly speaking, only what had already been threatened in Deu 28:49. (cf., Deu 32:21.), though here it assumes a more plastic form, and is here presented for the first time to the view of the prophet as though coming out of a mist. Jehovah summons the nations afar off: <hi type="italic">haggōyim</hi> <hi type="italic">mērâchok</hi> signifies, as we have rendered it, the “distant nations,” for <hi type="italic">mērâc</hi> is virtually an adjective both here and <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">Isa 49:1</reference>, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.23">Jer 23:23</reference> it is virtually a substantive. The visible working of Jehovah presents itself to the prophet in two figures. Jehovah plants a banner or standard, which, like an optical telegraph, announces to the nations at a more remote distance than the horn of battle (<hi type="italic">shophâr</hi>) could possibly reach, that they are to gather together to war. A “banner” (<hi type="italic">nês</hi>): i.e., a lofty staff with flying colours (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.23">Isa 33:23</reference>) planted upon a bare mountain-top (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Isa 13:2</reference>). נשׂא alternates with הרים in this favourite figure of Isaiah. The nations through whom this was primarily fulfilled were the nations of the Assyrian empire. According to the Old Testament view, these nations were regarded as far off, and dwelling at the end of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.3">Isa 39:3</reference>), not only inasmuch as the Euphrates formed the boundary towards the north-east between what was geographically known and unknown to the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference>; Zec 9:10), but also inasmuch as the prophet had in his mind a complex body of nations stretching far away into further Asia. The second figure is taken from a bee-master, who entices the bees, by hissing or whistling, to come out of their hives and settle on the ground. Thus Virgil says to the bee-master who wants to make the bees settle, “Raise a ringing, and beat the cymbals of Cybele all around” (<hi type="italic">Georgics</hi>, iv 54). Thus does Jehovah entice the hosts of nations like swarms of bees (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>), and they swarm together with haste and swiftness. The plural changes into the singular, because those who are approaching have all the appearance at first of a compact and indivisible mass; it is also possible that the ruling nation among the many is singled out. The thought and expression are both misty, and this is perfectly characteristic. With the word “behold” (<hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi>) the prophet points to them; they are approaching <hi type="italic">mehērâh</hi> <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, i.e., in the shortest time with swift feet, and the nearer they come to his view the more clearly he can describe them.
entries.d8f4f2c894a0a150e1b6a698feac133c300df651: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Isa 5:27</reference> <hi type="italic">“There is none exhausted, and none stumbling among them: it gives itself no slumber, and no sleep; and to none is the girdle of his hips loosed; and to none is the lace of his shoes broken.”</hi> Notwithstanding the long march, there is no exhausted one, obliged to separate himself and remain behind (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.18">Deu 25:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">Isa 14:31</reference>); no stumbling one (<hi type="italic">Cōshēl</hi>), for they march on, pressing incessantly forwards, as if along a well-made road (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.9">Jer 31:9</reference>). They do not slumber (<hi type="italic">nūm</hi>), to say nothing of sleeping (<hi type="italic">yâshēn</hi>), so great is their eagerness for battle: i.e., they do not slumber to refresh themselves, and do not even allow themselves their ordinary night’s rest. No one has the girdle of his armour-shirt or coat of mail, in which he stuck his sword (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.18">Neh 4:18</reference>), at all loosened; nor has a single one even the shoe-string, with which his sandals were fastened, <hi type="italic">broken</hi> (<hi type="italic">nittak, disrumpitur</hi>). The statement as to their want of rest forms a <hi type="italic">climax descendens</hi>; the other, as to the tightness and durability of their equipment, a <hi type="italic">climax ascendens</hi>: the two statements follow one another after the nature of a <hi type="italic">chiasmus</hi>.
entries.d4dfd3fc0dc6cebf0319101004da4fe2a51c7e2e: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.28">Isa 5:28</reference> <div eID="gen12872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12873" type="x-p"/> The prophet then proceeds to describe their weapons and war-chariots. <hi type="italic">“He whose arrows are sharpened, and all his bows strung; the hoofs of his horses are counted like flint, and his wheels like the whirlwind.”</hi> In the prophet’s view they are coming nearer and nearer. For he sees that they have brought the sharpened arrows in their quivers (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Isa 22:6</reference>); and the fact that all their bows are already <hi type="italic">trodden</hi> (namely, as their length was equal to a man’s height, by treading upon the string with the left foot, as we may learn from Arrian’s <hi type="italic">Indica</hi>), proves that they are near to the goal. The correct reading in Jablonsky (according to Kimchi’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>. cf., <hi type="italic">Michlal yofi</hi>) is קשּׁתתיו with <hi type="italic">dagesh dirimens</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.15">Psa 37:15</reference> (Ges. §20, 2,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). As the custom of shoeing horses was not practised in ancient times, firm hoofs (ὃπλαι καρτεραί, according to Xenophon’s <hi type="italic">Hippikos</hi>) were one of the most important points in a good horse. And the horses of the enemy that was now drawing near to Judah had hoofs that would be found like flint (<hi type="italic">tzar</hi>, only used here, equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">zirr</hi>). Homer designates such horses <hi type="italic">Chalkopodes</hi>, brazen-footed. And the two wheels of the war-chariots, to which they were harnessed, turned with such velocity, and overthrew everything before them with such violence, that it seemed not merely as if a whirlwind drove them forward, but as if they were the whirlwind itself (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jer 4:13</reference>). Nahum compares them to lightning (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Isa 2:5</reference>). Thus far the prophet’s description has moved on, as if by forced marches, in clauses of from two to four words each. It now changes into a heavy, stealthy pace, and then in a few clauses springs like a wild beast upon its prey.
entries.68c4d9992bc9ec288a13a482f173be646f3f1dd1: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">Isa 5:29</reference> <hi type="italic">“Roaring issues from it as from the lioness: it roars like lions, and utters a low murmur; seizes the prey, carries it off, and no one rescues.”</hi> The futures, with the preceding לו שׁאגה which is equivalent to a future, hold each feature in the description fast, as if for prolonged contemplation. The lion roars when eager for prey; and such is now the war-cry of the bloodthirsty enemy, which the prophet compares to the roaring of a lion or of young lions (<hi type="italic">Cephirim</hi>) in the fulness of their strength. (The lion is described by its poetic name, לביא; this does not exactly apply to the lioness, which would rather be designated by the term לביּה.) The roar is succeeded by a low growl (<hi type="italic">nâham</hi>, <hi type="italic">fremere</hi>), when a lion is preparing to fall upon its prey.<note placement="foot">In Arabic, <hi type="italic">en - nehem</hi> is used to signify greediness (see Ali’s <hi type="italic">Proverbs</hi>, No. 16).</note> <div eID="gen12873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12874" type="x-p"/> And so the prophet hears a low and ominous murmur in the army, which is now ready for battle. But he also sees immediately afterwards how the enemy seizes its booty and carries it irrecoverably away: literally, “how he causes it to escape,” i.e., not “lets it slip in cruel sport,” as Luzzatto interprets it, but carries it to a place of safety (Mic 6:14). The prey referred to is Judah. It also adds to the gloomy and mysterious character of the prophecy, that the prophet never mentions Judah. In the following v. also (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.30">Isa 5:30</reference>) the object is still suppressed, as if the prophet could not let it pass his lips.
entries.bcb757113ceb98f6c22446a2a5b4c6a57913586f: <reference osisRef="Isa.5.30">Isa 5:30</reference> <hi type="italic">“And it utters a deep roar over it in that day like the roaring of the sea: and it looks to the earth, and behold darkness, tribulation, and light; it becomes night over it in the clouds of heaven.”</hi> The subject to “roars” is the mass of the enemy; and in the expressions “over it” and “it looks” (<hi type="italic">nibbat</hi>; the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, which is only met with here, in the place of the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>) the prophet has in his mind the nation of Judah, upon which the enemy falls with the roar of the ocean - that is to say, overwhelming it like a sea. And when the people of Judah look to the earth, i.e., to their own land, darkness alone presents itself, and darkness which has swallowed up all the smiling and joyous aspect which it had before. And what then? The following words, <hi type="italic">tzar</hi> <hi type="italic">vâ'ōr</hi>, have been variously rendered, viz., “moon (= <hi type="italic">sahar</hi>) and sun” by the Jewish expositors, “stone and flash,” i.e., hail and thunder-storm, by Drechsler; but such renderings as these, and others of a similar kind, are too far removed from the ordinary usage of the language. And the separation of the two words, so that the one closes a sentence and the other commences a fresh one (e.g., “darkness of tribulation, and the sun becomes dark”), which is adopted by Hitzig, Gesenius, Ewald, and others, is opposed to the impression made by the two monosyllables, and sustained by the pointing, that they are connected together. The simplest explanation is one which takes the word <hi type="italic">tzar</hi> in its ordinary sense of tribulation or oppression, and <hi type="italic">'ōr</hi> in its ordinary sense of light, and which connects the two words closely together. And this is the case with the rendering given above: <hi type="italic">tzar</hi> <hi type="italic">vâ'ōr</hi> are “tribulation and brightening up,” one following the other and passing over into the other, like morning and night (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa 21:12</reference>). This pair of words forms an interjectional clause, the meaning of which is, that when the predicted darkness had settled upon the land of Judah, this would not be the end; but there would still follow an alternation of anxiety and glimmerings of hope, until at last it had become altogether dark in the cloudy sky over all the land of Judah (<hi type="italic">‛ariphim</hi>, the cloudy sky, is only met with here; it is derived from <hi type="italic">âraph</hi>, to drop or trickle, hence also <hi type="italic">arâphel</hi>: the suffix points back to <hi type="italic">lâ'âretz</hi>, <hi type="italic">eretz</hi> denoting sometimes the earth as a whole, and at other times the land as being part of the earth). The prophet here predicts that, before utter ruin has overtaken Judah, sundry approaches will be made towards this, within which a divine deliverance will appear again and again. Grace tries and tries again and again, until at last the measure of iniquity is full, and the time of repentance past. The history of the nation of Judah proceeded according to this law until the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. The Assyrian troubles, and the miraculous light of divine help which arose in the destruction of the military power of Sennacherib, were only the foreground of this mournful but yet ever and anon hopeful course of history, which terminated in utter darkness, that has continued now for nearly two thousand years. <div eID="gen12874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12875" type="x-p"/> This closes the third prophetic address. It commences with a parable which contains the history of Israel <hi type="italic">in nuce</hi>, and closes with an emblem which symbolizes the gradual but yet certain accomplishment of the judicial, penal termination of the parable. This third address, therefore, is as complete in itself as the second was. The kindred allusions are to be accounted for from the sameness of the historical basis and arena. During the course of the exposition, it has become more and more evident and certain that it relates to the time of Uzziah and Jotham - a time of peace, of strength, and wealth, but also of pride and luxury. The terrible slaughter of the Syro-Ephraimitish war, which broke out at the end of Jotham’s reign, and the varied complications which king Ahaz introduced between Judah and the imperial worldly power, and which issued eventually in the destruction of the former kingdom - those five marked epochs in the history of the kingdoms of the world, or great empires, to which the Syro-Ephraimitish war was the prelude - were still hidden from the prophet in the womb of the future. The description of the great mass of people that was about to roll over Judah from afar is couched in such general terms, so undefined and misty, that all we can say is, that everything that was to happen to the people of God on the part of the imperial power during the five great and extended periods of judgment that were now so soon to commence (viz., the Assyrian, the Chaldean, the Persian, the Grecian, and the Roman), was here unfolding itself out of the mist of futurity, and presenting itself to the prophet’s eye. Even in the time of Ahaz the character of the prophecy changed in this respect. It was then that the eventful relation, in which Israel stood to the imperial power, generally assumed its first concrete shape in the form of a distinct relation to Asshur (Assyria). And from that time forth the imperial power in the mouth of the prophet is no longer a majestic thing without a name; but although the notion of the imperial power was not yet embodied in Asshur, it was called Asshur, and Asshur stood as its representative. It also necessarily follows from this, that Chapters 2-4 and 5 belong to the times anterior to Ahaz, i.e., to those of Uzziah and Jotham. But several different questions suggest themselves here. If chapters 2-4 and 5 were uttered under Uzziah and Jotham, how could Isaiah begin with a promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:1-4</reference>) which is repeated word for word in Mic 4:1., where it is the direct antithesis to <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference>, which was uttered by Micah, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference>, in the time of Hezekiah? Again, if we consider the advance apparent in the predictions of judgment from the general expressions with which they commence in Chapter 1 to the close of chapter 5, in what relation does the address in chapter 1 stand to chapters 2-4 and 5, inasmuch as <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7-Isa.5.9">Isa 5:7-9</reference> are not ideal (as we felt obliged to maintain, in opposition to Caspari), but have a distinct historical reference, and therefore at any rate presuppose the Syro-Ephraimitish war? And lastly, if <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> does really relate, as it apparently does, to the call of Isaiah to the prophetic office, how are we to explain the singular fact, that three prophetic addresses precede the history of his call, which ought properly to stand at the commencement of the book? Drechsler and Caspari have answered this question lately, by maintaining that <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> does not contain an account of the call of Isaiah to the prophetic office, but simply of the call of the prophet, who was already installed in that office, to one particular mission. The proper heading to be adopted for <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> would therefore be, <hi type="italic">“The ordination of the prophet as the preacher of the judgment of hardening;”</hi> and chapters 1-5 would contain warning reproofs addressed by the prophet to the people, who were fast ripening for this judgment of hardening (reprobation), for the purpose of calling them to repentance. The final decision was still trembling in the balance. But the call to repentance was fruitless, and Israel hardened itself. And now that the goodness of God had tried in vain to lead the people to repentance, and the long-suffering of God had been wantonly abused by the people, Jehovah Himself would harden them. Looked at in this light, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> stands in its true historical place. It contains the divine sequel to that portion of Isaiah’s preaching, and of the prophetic preaching generally, by which it had been preceded. But true as it is that the whole of the central portion of Israel’s history, which lay midway between the commencement and the close, was divided in half by the contents of <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference>, and that the distinctive importance of Isaiah as a prophet arose especially from the fact that he stood upon the boundary between these two historic halves; there are serious objections which present themselves to such an explanation of <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>-13. It is possible, indeed, that this distinctive importance may have been given to Isaiah’s official position at his very first call. And what Umbreit says - namely, that <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> must make the impression upon every unprejudiced mind, that it relates to the prophet’s inaugural vision - cannot really be denied. but the position in which <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> stands in the book itself must necessarily produce a contrary impression, unless it can be accounted for in some other way. Nevertheless the impression still remains (just as at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:7-9</reference>), and recurs again and again. We will therefore proceed to <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> without attempting to efface it. It is possible that we may discover some other satisfactory explanation of the enigmatical position of <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> in relation to what precedes.  <chapter eID="Isa.5"/> <div eID="gen12875" type="x-p"/>

entries.7131b103c731849678addefcbf59d98ba2d3918d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.5.1" sID="gen41007" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Now will I sing to my beloved.</hi> The subject of this chapter is different from that of the former. It was the design of the Prophet to describe the condition of the people of Israel, as it then was, in order that all might perceive their faults, and might thus be led by shame and self-loathing to sincere repentance. Here, as in a mirror, the people might behold the misery of their condition. But for this, they would have flattered themselves too much in their crimes, and would not have patiently listened to any instructions. It was therefore necessary to present a striking and lively picture of their wickedness; and in order that it might have the greater weight, he made use of this preface; for great and memorable events were usually described in verse, that they might be repeated by every one, and that a lasting record of them might be preserved. In like manner, we see that Moses wrote a song, and many other compositions, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.15.1">Exodus 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.1">Deuteronomy 32:1</reference>,) in order that all the events might be proclaimed in this manner, both in public and in private. The instruction becomes more widely diffused than if it had been delivered in plainer language. For the same reason Isaiah composed this song, that he might present to the people a clearer view of their wickedness; and, undoubtedly, he handled this subject with magnificent and harmonious language, for the highest skill is commonly exercised in the composition of poems.<div eID="gen41008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41009" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To my beloved.</hi> There can be no doubt that he means God; as if he had said that he would compose a poem in behalf of God, that he might expostulate with the people about their ingratitude; for it gave additional weight to his language to represent God as speaking. But a question arises, Why does Isaiah call God his friend? Some reply that he was a kinsman of Christ, and I acknowledge that he was a descendant of David; but this appears to be a forced interpretation. A more natural and appropriate one would be, to adopt the statement of John, that the Church is committed to <hi type="italic">the friends of the bridegroom</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.29">John 3:29</reference>,) and to reckon prophets as belonging to that class. To them, unquestionably, this designation applies; for the ancient people were placed under their charge, that they might be kept under their leader. We need not wonder, therefore, that they were jealous and were greatly offended when the people bestowed their attachment on any other. Isaiah therefore assumes the character of the bridegroom, and, being deeply anxious about the bride entrusted to him, complains that she has broken conjugal fidelity, and deplores her treachery and ingratitude.<div eID="gen41009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41010" type="x-p"/>Hence we learn that not only Paul, but all those prophets and teachers who faithfully served God, were jealous of God’s spouse. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.2">2 Corinthians 11:2</reference>.) And all the servants of God ought to be greatly moved and aroused by this appellation; for what does a man reckon more valuable than his wife? A well-disposed husband will value her more highly than all his treasures, and will more readily commit to any person the charge of his wealth than of his wife. He to whom one will entrust his dearly-beloved wife must be reckoned very faithful. Now to pastors and ministers the Lord commits his Church as his beloved wife. How great will be our wickedness if we betray her by sloth and negligence! Whosoever does not labor earnestly to preserve her can on no pretense be excused.<div eID="gen41010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41011" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">A song of my beloved.</hi> By using the word <foreign xml:lang="he">דודי</foreign>, <hi type="italic">dodi</hi>, he changes the first syllable, but the meaning is the same as in the former clause. Though some render it <hi type="italic">uncle</hi>, and others <hi type="italic">cousin</hi>, I rather agree with those who consider it to contain an allusion; for greater liberties are allowed to poets than to other writers. By his arrangement of those words, and by his allusions to them, he intended that the sound and rhythm should aid the memory, and impress the minds, of his readers.<div eID="gen41011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41012" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">My beloved had a vineyard.</hi> The metaphor of <hi type="italic">a vineyard</hi> is frequently employed by the prophets, and it would be impossible to find a more appropriate comparison. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.80.8">Psalm 80:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.21">Jeremiah 2:21</reference>.) There are two ways in which it points out how highly the Lord values his Church; for no possession is dearer to a man than <hi type="italic">a vineyard</hi>, and there is none that demands more constant and persevering toil. Not only, therefore, does the Lord declare that we are his beloved inheritance, but at the same time points out his care and anxiety about us.<div eID="gen41012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41013" type="x-p"/>In this <hi type="italic">song</hi> the Prophet mentions, first, the benefits which the Lord had bestowed on the Jewish people; secondly, he explains how great was the ingratitude of the people; thirdly, the punishment which must follow; fourthly, he enumerates the vices of the people; for men never acknowledge their vices till they are compelled to do so.<div eID="gen41013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41014" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">On a hill.</hi> He begins by saying that God had placed his people in a favorable situation, as when a person plants a vine on a pleasant and fertile hill. By the word <hi type="italic">horn</hi> or <hi type="italic">hill</hi> I understand a lofty place rising above a plain, or what we commonly call <hi type="italic">a rising-ground</hi>, (<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">un coustau</hi></foreign>.) It is supposed by some to refer to the situation of Jerusalem, but I consider this to be unnatural and forced. It rather belongs to the construction of the Prophet’s allegory; and as God was pleased to take this people under his care and protection, he compares this favor <hi type="italic">to the planting of a vineyard;</hi> for it is better to plant vines on hills and lofty places than on a plain. In like manner the poet says, <hi type="italic">The vine loves the open hills; the yews prefer the north wind and the cold</hi> <note n="75"> <div sID="gen41015" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Denique apertos Bacchus amat colles: Aquilonem et frigora taxi</foreign>. <hi type="italic">Virg, Georg</hi>. II. 112.<div eID="gen41015" type="x-p"/> </note> The Prophet, therefore, having alluded to the ordinary method of planting the vine, next follows out the comparison, that this place occupied no ordinary situation. When he calls it <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">son of oil</hi> or <hi type="italic">of fatness</hi>, <note n="76"> <div sID="gen41016" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> In a very fruitful hill</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen41016" type="x-p"/> </note> he means a rich and exceedingly fertile spot. This is limited by some commentators to the fertility of Judea, but that does not accord with my views, for the Prophet intended to describe metaphorically the prosperous condition of the people.<div eID="gen41014" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen41007" osisID="Isa.5.1" type="section"/>
entries.fb26a7127f6a4ca13665cc51f490474a2b64406a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.5.2" sID="gen41017" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he fenced it.</hi> The incessant care and watchfulness of God in dressing his vine are asserted by the Prophet, as if he had said, that God has neglected nothing that could be expected from the best and most careful householder. And yet we do not choose to attempt, as some commentators have done, an ingenious exposition of every clause, such as, that the Church is <hi type="italic">fenced</hi> by the protection of the Holy Spirit, so that it is safe against the attacks of the devil; that the <hi type="italic">wine-press</hi> is doctrine; and that by <hi type="italic">the stones</hi> are meant the annoyances of errors. The design of the Prophet, as I have mentioned, was more obvious, namely, that by incessant care and large expenditure God has performed the part of an excellent husbandman. Yet it was the duty of the Jews to consider how numerous and diversified were the blessings which God had conferred on them; and at the present day, when the Church is represented under the metaphor of <hi type="italic">a vineyard</hi>, we ought to view those figures as denoting God’s blessings, by which he makes known not only his love toward us, but likewise his solicitude about our salvation.<div eID="gen41018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41019" type="x-p"/>In the verb <hi type="italic">planted</hi> the order appears to be reversed, for one ought to begin with <hi type="italic">planting</hi> rather than with the <hi type="italic">fence</hi>; but my explanation is, that after having <hi type="italic">planted</hi>, he did everything else that was necessary. Justly, therefore, does he charge them with ingratitude and treachery, when the fruits that ought to have followed such laborious cultivation were not brought forth. There is reason to fear that the Lord will bring the same accusation against us; for the greater the benefits which we have received from God, the more disgraceful will be our ingratitude if we abuse them. It is not without a good reason, or to enable them to make any idle display, that the Lord blesses his people; it is, that they may yield <hi type="italic">grapes</hi>, that is, the best fruit. If he be disappointed of his expectation, the punishment which the Prophet here describes will follow. The mention of his benefits ought, therefore, to produce a powerful impression on our minds, and to excite us to gratitude.<div eID="gen41019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41020" type="x-p"/>Besides, the word <hi type="italic">vineyard</hi>, and a <hi type="italic">vineyard</hi> so carefully cultivated, suggests an implied contrast; for so much the more highly ought we to value the acts of God’s kindness, when they are not of an ordinary description, but tokens of his peculiar regard. Other blessings are indiscriminately bestowed, such as, that he<div eID="gen41020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41021" type="x-p"/>maketh the sun to shine on the evil as well as on the good, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.45">Matthew 5:45</reference>,)<div eID="gen41021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41022" type="x-p"/>and supplies them with what is necessary for food and clothing. But how much more highly ought we to esteem that covenant of grace into which he has entered with us, by which he makes the light of the Gospel to shine on us; for his own people are its peculiar objects! That care and diligence, therefore, which the Lord continually manifests in cultivating our minds deserves our most earnest consideration.<div eID="gen41022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41023" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Therefore he hoped that it would bring forth grapes</hi> <note n="77"> <div sID="gen41024" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> And he looked that it should bring forth grapes</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen41024" type="x-p"/> </note> He now complains that the nation which had enjoyed such high advantages had basely and shamefully degenerated; and he accuses them of undervaluing the kindness of God, for he says that, instead of <hi type="italic">pleasant grapes</hi>, they yielded only <hi type="italic">wild</hi> and bitter fruits. It is undoubtedly true that God, to whose eyes <hi type="italic">all things are naked and opened</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.13">Hebrew 4:13</reference>,) is not deceived by his expectation like a mortal man. In the Song of Moses he plainly declares that he well knew from the beginning what would be the wickedness of his people.<div eID="gen41023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41025" type="x-p"/>My beloved, says he, when she fares well and becomes fat,<lb/> will kick. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.15">Deuteronomy 32:15</reference>.)<div eID="gen41025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41026" type="x-p"/>It is therefore not more possible that God should be mistaken in his expectations, than that he should repent. Isaiah does not here enter into subtle reasonings about the expectations which God had formed, but describes the manner in which the people ought to have acted, that they might not lose the benefit of such excellent advantages. Thus God commands that the Gospel be proclaimed <hi type="italic">for the obedience of</hi> <hi type="italic">faith</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.26">Romans 16:26</reference>,) not that he expects all to be obedient, but because, by the mere hearing of it, unbelievers are rendered inexcusable.
