Even though we think that we are defended on all sides by friends, yet God will stir up enemies from the farthest corners of the earth, who will break through every obstruction, and overtake us with ease, as if the way were plain and smooth. This ought to be carefully observed, that we may not suffer ourselves to be blinded by vain presumption and foolish confidence.
We ought also to observe that wars are not kindled accidentally, or by an arrangement of men, but by the command of God, as if he assembled the soldiers by the sound of a trumpet. Whether, therefore, we are afflicted by battle, or by famine, or by pestilence, let us know that all this comes from the hand of God, for all things obey him and follow his direction. And yet it was not the intention of the Chaldeans to obey God, for they were hurried on by their eagerness to obtain wealth and power, while he has quite another object in view: but God employs their agency for executing his judgments. Hence arises a remarkable and illustrious display of the power of God, which is not limited by the will of men, or dependent on their decisions, but leads them, though contrary to their wish, or without their knowledge, to obey him. And yet it is no excuse for the ungodly that they are drawn contrary to the disposition of their mind, and do not willingly serve God, for they aim at nothing else than fraud, cruelty, and violence; and by their cruelty God punishes the transgressions and crimes of his people.
entries.79633b650878e8edf5c105489740638fcfd6aefe: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.5.27" sID="gen41158" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">None shall be weary, nor stumble among them.</hi> The meaning is, that everything will be prepared and arranged in such a manner that there shall be no delay or obstruction to their march; as if a prince, having recruited the ranks of his soldiers, immediately gave orders that the roads should be cleared, provisions obtained, and everything necessary provided. He therefore shows that they will be fleet and swift, and that there will be nothing to hinder their rapid march.<div eID="gen41159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41160" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">None shall slumber nor sleep.</hi> He expresses their vast activity by saying that they will not be drowsy. In these words, <hi type="italic">they shall not slumber nor sleep</hi>, the natural order is inverted, He ought rather to have said, <hi type="italic">They shall not sleep nor slumber</hi>; for it is a smaller matter to <hi type="italic">slumber</hi> than to <hi type="italic">sleep</hi>. But that phrase ought to be explained in this manner: <hi type="italic">They shall not slumber nor even sleep</hi>; that is, they will be so far from <hi type="italic">sleeping</hi>, that they will not even <hi type="italic">slumber</hi>. You have an instance of this in these words:<div eID="gen41160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41161" type="x-p"/>Lo, he that keepeth Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.121.4">Psalm 121:4</reference>.)<div eID="gen41161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41162" type="x-p"/>It is a Hebrew phrase, with which neither the Greek nor the Latin idiom agrees.<div eID="gen41162" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen41158" osisID="Isa.5.27" type="section"/>
entries.cdbfff0a0bcb12fb3d9486f76a296b6b896db3ed: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.5.28" sID="gen41163" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">Their arrows will be sharp.</hi> He means that they will be provided with necessary weapons. The custom alluded to is that which existed among the Assyrians and other eastern nations, who frequently made use of bows and arrows in battle, as Englishmen of the present day enter into the battlefield with a loaded quiver. <note n="90"> <div sID="gen41165" type="x-p"/> More than three hundred years have elapsed since Calvin wrote these words, and <hi type="italic">Englishmen of the present day</hi> do not carry bows and arrows into the field of battle. On the whole subject of war the opinions of Englishmen are underdoing an important revolution. Many of them entertain a confident hope that ere long the bullet as well as the arrow, the cannon as well as the bow, will be laid aside; that the revolting spectacle of human beings drawn up in companies, for the purpose of wholesale murder, will disappear from the earth; and that men will <hi type="italic">beat their swords into</hi> <hi type="italic">plough-shares, and their spears into pruning-hooks; nation</hi> <hi type="italic">shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they</hi> <hi type="italic">learn war any more</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen41165" type="x-p"/> </note> Under this class he includes every kind of weapons of war. But as the way was long, and the journey difficult, the Jew might think that many things would occur to interrupt the march of the enemy. He therefore says, that <hi type="italic">the hoofs of the horses will be like flint</hi>; by which he means that they will suffer no molestation, and will at length arrive in Judea without weariness. For a similar reason he compares <hi type="italic">their wheels to a whirlwind</hi>. The ancients were wont to employ chariots in going to war, and therefore he mentions not only <hi type="italic">horses</hi>, but <hi type="italic">wheels</hi>. All these circumstances must be understood to relate to the haste and rapidity with which they would proceed; or, in other words, that no length of journey would prevent the Lord from carrying forward the enemies without delay for the destruction of the Jews.<div eID="gen41164" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen41163" osisID="Isa.5.28" type="section"/>
entries.bb2b0930c8aa4555ceb64c7dfec7ab01471c3399: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.5.29" sID="gen41166" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">His roaring shall be like that of a lion.</hi> This denotes fierceness and cruelty, for he compares the Chaldeans to <hi type="italic">lions</hi>, which, we know, are frightful to behold, and savage by nature; as if he had said that they would not be men who were moved by any feeling of compassion or tenderness, but rather that they would be savage beasts. He adds, that they will likewise possess great strength, so that none will venture to approach for rescuing their prey. He means that the Jews will have no defense for warding off their attacks, because the dread of their cruelty will keep all at a distance from them. It was God who employed their agency in punishing the Jews, and therefore it was necessary that they should be armed with formidable power, that this wayward people might at length acknowledge that they had to do not with men but with<div eID="gen41167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41168" type="x-p"/>God, into whose hands it is a fearful thing to fall.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.31">Hebrews 10:31</reference>.)<div eID="gen41168" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.5.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen41166" osisID="Isa.5.29" type="section"/>
entries.795f601618dc88e8e293db9dd8359cbe6e6dcdf2:
30. He shall roar against him.
And in that day they shall roar against them. — Eng. Ver.
The Prophet adds this, that the Jews may understand that the fierce attack of the Chaldeans is not accidental, but that they have been appointed by God and are guided by his hand. By the roaring of the sea he means an attack so violent that it will look like a deluge, by which the whole of Judea will suffer shipwreck. He likewise cuts off all hope by foretelling that the punishment will have no alleviation and no end. “The Jews,” he says, “will do what is usually done in a season of perplexity, will cast their eyes up and down to discover the means of escape; but in whatever direction they look, whether to heaven or to earth, they will find no relief whatever; for on all sides distresses and calamities will overwhelm them.” This mode of expression has come to be frequently employed even by the common people, when misery and ruin appear on all sides, and no escape or relief can be found. This must unavoidably happen when the Lord pursues us, so that his uplifted arm meets our eyes on every side, and, wherever we turn, we behold his creatures armed against us to execute his judgments; for we may sometimes escape the hand of men, but how can we escape the hand of God?
CHAPTER 6.
Isaiah Chapter 6:1-13
1. In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.
1. Anno mortis regis Usiae, vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum et elevatum, cujus extrema replebant templum.
2. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly.
2. Et seraphim stabant super ipsum: erant singulis sex alae; duabus operiebant faciem suam; duabus tegebant pedes suos; et duabus volabant.
3. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
3. Et clamabant alter alteri, dicentes, Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Iehova exercituum; plena est omnis terra gloriae ejus.
4. And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke.
4. Et commota sunt superliminaria postium a voce clamantis; et domus impleta est fumo.
5. Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.
5. Tunc dixi, Vae mihi, quia excisus sum (vel in silentium redactus); cum homo sim pollutis labiis, et in medio populi habitem polluta labia habentis; et tamen regem Iehovam exercituum viderunt oculi mei.
6. Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the alter:
6. Volavit autem ad me unus ex seraphim; habens in manu sua carbonem ardentem, forcipe correptum ab altari.
7. And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.
7. Et applicans super os meum, dixit, Ecce, tetigit hoc labia tua, et expiabitur peccatum tuum.
8. Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
8. Postea audivi vocem Domini dicentis, Quem mittam? et quis ibit nobis? Tum dixi, Ecce ego, mitte me.
9. And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not.
9. Tum dixit, Vade, et dic populo isti; audiendo audite, et ne intelligatis; videndo videto, et nesciatis;
10. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed.
10. Obstina cor populi hujus, et aures ejus aggrava, et oculos ejus obline; ne forte videat oculis suis, et auribus suis audiat, et cor ejus intelligat, et ubi conversus fuerit, sit illi sanatio.
11. Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate,
11. Et dixi, Usque quo, Domine? et ait, Dum fuerint vastatae civitates absque habitatore, et domus vacuatae fuerint hominibus, et terra redacta fuerit in solitudinem;
12. And the Lord have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land.
12. Donec procul amoverit Deus homines, sitque multa vastitas in medio terrae;
13. But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil-tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves, so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.
13. Donec in ea decima, et revertetur; et erit in excidium sicut tilia et quercus, quibus in projectione est subsistentia; ita in hac erit subsistentia, semen sanctum.

                        </ns0:gap> poor and harmless People, who shall be left in the Land when the Rich are carried into Captivity, as it fell out 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25. 12.</ns0:note> feed after their manner <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>by their fold,</ns0:hi> as this Word is mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />festly used <ns0:hi>Mic.</ns0:hi> 2. 12. the onely place of Scripture, except this, in which this Word is found.</ns0:note>, and the waste places <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Lands left by their Owners, who were either slain, or carried into Capti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vity.</ns0:note> of the fat ones <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of the Rich and Great men, so called <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22. 29. & 78. 31. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10. 16.</ns0:note> shall strangers <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The poor <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who were <ns0:hi>left to be vine-dressers and husbandmen,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25. 12. who are called <ns0:hi>strangers,</ns0:hi> because they were so in reference to that Land, not being the proper Owners of it, nor related to them; as the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> of other Tribes are called <ns0:hi>strangers,</ns0:hi> in opposition to the <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 1. 51. and elsewhere; yea, and the <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> are so called, in opposition to the Seed of <ns0:hi>Aaron, Numb.</ns0:hi> 16. 40.</ns0:note> eat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Wo unto them that draw iniquity <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That are not onely drawn to sin by the Allurements of the World, or by the Perswasions of wicked men, being sur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prised and overtaken by Sin, as sometimes good men are, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6. 1. but are active and industrious in drawing Sin to themselves, or themselves to Sin; that greedily and steadily pursue Sin, and the Occasions of it, and are not at rest till they have overtaken it; that sin wilfully, and resolvedly, and industriously.</ns0:note> with cords of vanity <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>with cords of lying,</ns0:hi> as the last Word frequently signifies, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with vain and deceitful Arguments and Pretences, whereby Sinners generally draw themselves to Sin; among which, one follows in the next Verse, to wit, the Impunity which they promise to themselves. Or these Cords may note the Means which they use to accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plish that Iniquity which they have devised.</ns0:note>, and sin as it were with a cart<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rope <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">With all their might, as Beasts commonly do that draw Carts with Ropes.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 17. 15, Amos 5. 18. 2 Pet. 3. 3, 4.</ns0:note> That say, Let him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, God, in whose Name thou and other Prophets are always reproving and threatning us.</ns0:note> make speed, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sten his work, that we may see <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He onely thinks to affright us with Bugbears; but he either cannot, or will not do us any harm: we do not fear him, let him do his worst, let him begin as soon as he pleaseth. Not that any of the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were so impudent as to use these Expressions; but this was the plain Language of their Actions, they lived as if they were of this Opinion; their Presumption and Secu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity shewed their desperate Contempt of God, and of all his Judgments.</ns0:note>: and let the counsel of the holy One of Israel <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Who by his <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> is engaged to pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nish us. They scornfully repeated the Title usually given by the Prophets unto God.</ns0:note> draw nigh and come, that we may know <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Wo unto them <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that say concerning e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil, <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> that call evil good, and good evil <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That take away the difference between Good and Evil, that justifie and approve wicked Men and Things, and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demn Piety, or Vertue, or righteous Persons. Compare <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 17. 15. Thus many call Serious Godliness, Humour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Singularity; and Justice, Morofity; and Meekness, Stu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pidity, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> as on the contrary<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> call Pride, Magnanimi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty; and Covetousness, Good<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>andry. And men are very apt to follow the Course of the World in their false Judgments of things; which therefore the Prophet so se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verely forbids.</ns0:note>; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Wo unto <ns0:hi>them that are</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 7. Rom. 12. 16.</ns0:note> wise in their own eyes, and prudent <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> before their face.</ns0:note> in their own sight <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">That being puffed up with an Opinion of their own Wisdom, despise the Counsels and Instructions of God by his Prophets, and prefer their own vain Fancies before the Judgment of the All-wise God, as appears by the Errour beforementioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. that they affirmed that to be Evil, which God had declared to be Good.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Wo unto <ns0:hi>them that are</ns0:hi> mighty to drink wine <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That can drink much without Intoxication, in which they gloried, as too many do at this day.</ns0:note>, and men of strength to mingle <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To drink: the Antecedent being put for the Consequent; which is usual: for they mingled it in order to drinking.</ns0:note> strong drink.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Which <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 17. 15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> & 24. 24.</ns0:note> justifie the wicked for reward <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not by mistake or incogitancy, but wilfully for Bribes.</ns0:note>, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, juridically, they pronounce Sentence against him, as if he and his Cause were unjust.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Therefore as <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the tongue of fire.</ns0:note> the fire devoureth the stub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> their root shall be as rottenness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">They shall be like a Tree which not onely withers in its Branches, but dies and rots at the Roots, and therefore is past all hopes of recovery. The sence is, They shall be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyed both Root and Branch.</ns0:note>, and their blossom shall go up as dust <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Shall vanish (for so the Word <ns0:hi>ascend</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>go up</ns0:hi> is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16. 14. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 5. 26. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 15. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 11. 23, 24.) as the Dust, which is blown away with every Wind; or, shall be resolved into Dust, and yield no Fruit.</ns0:note>: because they have cast away <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which implies Disobedience joyned with Contempt.</ns0:note> the law of the LORD of hosts, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spised the word of the hole One of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:568" />25 Therefore is the anger of the LORD kin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">A Metaphorical and Hyperbolical Description of a grievous Calamity, familiar in the Prophets, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 64. 1, 2. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 4. 24. and in other Authors.</ns0:note>, and their car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cases <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> as dung.</ns0:note> torn in the midst of the streets. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 9. 12. & 17. 21. & 10. 4.</ns0:note> For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Ready to give you ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther and a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>orer Blow. This is not the end, as you vainly imagine; but, if you repent not, the beginning of your Sorrows, and an Earnest of further Calamities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And he will lift up an ensign <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To call them together for this Service, as Generals use to do for the raising of Armies.</ns0:note> to the nati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons from far <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, 1. to the <ns0:hi>Assyri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans,</ns0:hi> of whom he speaks more particularly <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 10. and that under this same Character of a People that <ns0:hi>come from far, v.</ns0:hi> 3. and who did not long after this Prophecy invade <ns0:hi>Iu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />daea,</ns0:hi> and did much mischief in it. Although that part of the Prediction, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29. <ns0:hi>they <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe, and none shall deliver it,</ns0:hi> do not seem to agree to them, nor that Invasion; for the <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> were forced to retreat with great shame and loss, and the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered from them. Or, 2. to the <ns0:hi>Chaldaeans;</ns0:hi> for even <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>a far countrey, Isa.</ns0:hi> 39. 3. And he saith <ns0:hi>nations,</ns0:hi> because the <ns0:hi>Chaldaean</ns0:hi> Army was made up of several Nati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons.</ns0:note>, and will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7. 18.</ns0:note> hiss unto them <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>will whistle unto,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>for them:</ns0:hi> will gather them together by his Word, as Shepherds gather their Sheep. He intimates how easily and speedily God can do this Work.</ns0:note> from the ends of the earth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which is not to be understood strictly, but popularly, and with a latitude, from very remote Places; although part of the <ns0:hi>Chaldaean</ns0:hi> Army did come from Places not very <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> distant from the end of that part of the World, so far as <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> was then known.</ns0:note>: and behold, they shall come with speed swiftly.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 None shall be weary <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Though their March be long and tedious. As I have called them to this Work, so I will strengthen and assist them in it.</ns0:note>, nor stumble amongst them: none shall slumber nor sleep <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">They shall all be watchful and diligent to take all Opportunities and Advantages of executing my Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments upon my People.</ns0:note>: neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which otherwise would hinder, or at least slacken them in their March. I will take all Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pediments out of their way.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 Whose arrows <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> sharp, and all their bows bent <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Who are every way furnished and ready for my Work, waiting onely for my Command.</ns0:note>: their horses hoofs shall be counted like flint <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Because they shall not be broken or battered by the length or stoniness and rug<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gedness of the Way.</ns0:note>, and their wheels like a whirlwind <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Partly for the swiftness of their March, and partly for the force and violence of their Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riots in Battel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Their roaring <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> like a lion, they shall roar like young lions <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which signifies both their Cruelty, and their greedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and eagerness to catch and devour the Prey.</ns0:note>; yea, they shall roar and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> away safe, and none <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> themselves, nor the <ns0:hi>Egyptians,</ns0:hi> to whose help they will trust, nor any of their Confederates.</ns0:note> shall deliver <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And in that day they shall roar against them, like the roaring of the sea <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Which is violent and frightful.</ns0:note>: and if <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8. 22.</ns0:note> look unto the land, behold, darkness and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> distress.</ns0:note> sor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Darkness, to wit, Sorrow; the latter Word explains the former, and the Particle <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> is put expositively, as it is frequently.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> when it is light, it shall be dark in the destructions thereof.</ns0:note> and the light is darkned in the heavens thereof <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">When they look up to the Heavens, as men in distress usually do, they see no Light there; their Comforts are wholly eclip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, and their Hopes are like the giving up of the Ghost.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
